Tennis player Novak Ðjoković: lifted off and landed hard Novak Ðjoković, number 1 in men's tennis, is currently probably the second most famous prisoner in the world behind Julien Assange. Although ""detainee"" is an exaggeration, at least according to the Australian government, under whose authority the Serbian is being held. After all, the ""Djoker"" is ""only serving a temporary sentence"" in a deportation hotel in Melbourne and ""can leave again at any time"", according to Australian Home Affairs Minister Karen Andrews. The fact that the Serb ticks differently than most is nothing new. The 20-time Grand Slam champion had phases in which he was coached by a ""guru""; during the first lockdown, he thought it was a good idea to organize a series of tournaments on the Adriatic, where several professionals and he himself were infected with corona. He did an egg dance around his participation in the Australian Open and his ""vaccination status"" because he knew that the tournament was to take place under 2G conditions. An egg dance that has brought him to where he is now. However, this impressive case of an unruly megastar offers so many twists and turns that the use of tennis metaphors seems obvious. It's a drama, a five-set match; or smaller: Ðjoković was passed hard, gave up his serve, but now, after a short break, still has every chance. Although it doesn't look good for him. There are so many levels and sides to this case that you can't keep up. On the one hand, there is the parallel world of top-class sport and one of its richest and most headstrong representatives; on the other, there is a harsh state that does not like to show itself to be cosmopolitan and foreign-friendly. We have corona entry rules that apply to everyone, which means that the other world formula, according to which the rich and people with influence can go anywhere, is suspended for a brief moment in history. We have a father who stands up for his son, from a nation that almost traditionally feels disadvantaged and does not shy away from conflict; we have protesters here and there. And in the middle of it all is Ðjoković, who is stuck in Melbourne alongside countless asylum seekers, waiting for the next court decision. Yet everything could be so simple. Even people like Rafael Nadal and Boris Becker, two other greats of ""white sport"", say so. But ""Novax"" prefers to remain unvaccinated ""in the best tradition of Balkan idiocy"" (according to the Croatian daily newspaper Jutarnji List) and play against windmills. Because as this case makes clear: the times when your own state of health was a private matter are unfortunately over.

Brexit: Government seeks way out in marathon meeting The British government met on Tuesday for crisis consultations on a way out of the Brexit impasse. A longer cabinet meeting is planned into the afternoon with different members. On Monday evening, Parliament once again failed to reach an agreement in a vote on alternatives to May's Brexit agreement. According to reports, the head of government could now present the withdrawal agreement she negotiated with the EU to MPs for a fourth time. Parliament will try again on Wednesday. However, a further round of votes in the House of Commons on alternatives to May's Brexit deal was initially planned for Wednesday. According to speculation, however, parliament could also try to force the government to extend the withdrawal deadline further. British Education Secretary Damian Hinds continues to back Prime Minister Theresa May's Brexit deal. ""The deal negotiated by the government is the most balanced and I hope and expect that's where we'll end up,"" Hinds said on BBC television. ""It's still by far the best option."" Negotiations with the EU will come one way or another. The EU wants to insist on the clarification of outstanding Brexit issues even in the event of a ""no deal"" scenario. However, if no agreement is reached, the atmosphere will be different, EU Brexit chief negotiator Michel Barnier told the European Parliament on Tuesday. ""A no deal is a breach of trust."" Even in the event of a disorderly, hard Brexit, it would not take long for the UK to request negotiations with the EU on trade, transport and other issues, Barnier said. The outstanding issues that were actually supposed to be settled in the withdrawal agreement, such as the Irish border, the final Brexit bill of around 39 billion pounds (45.44 billion euros) and the rights of EU citizens, would then come back into play. ""We will then put these questions back on the table,"" said Barnier. ECB sees financial sector well prepared. According to the head of the French central bank, Francois Villeroy de Galhau, the European financial sector is prepared for a hard Brexit. ""We have made all preparations at European and national level, including in the event of a no-deal exit, to ensure that contracts continue to be honored and that customers in the financial sector are protected,"" the ECB Governing Council member told ""France Inter Radio"". As things stand at present, Great Britain will enter the EU on 12. April from the European Union. If neither the withdrawal agreement nor an alternative is agreed by then, there is a threat of a no-deal exit with drastic consequences for the economy and many other areas of life.

Revocation of patent protection for vaccines: What industry and patent lawyers have to say Pfizer boss Albert Bourla is strictly opposed to the removal of patent protection, not least because this would not increase production. The difficult production process in mRNA technology is time-consuming and especially now, when time is of the essence, cannot be mastered simply by making changes to patent law. In order to process the 280 components currently used from 86 suppliers from 19 countries, complex special systems and trained personnel are required. Moderna boss Stéphane Bancel takes a similar view. The head of the US biotech company, which produces the second mRNA-based drug approved in the USA and the European Union, believes that patent approval this year or next will not really speed up availability. There is simply ""not enough talent in the world and not enough production facilities that can reliably guarantee complex production."" Even if all patents were indeed freely available, others would ""first have to develop their own manufacturing processes and have their product approved"". This also takes many months. BioNTech CEO Uğur Şahin believes that patents are not a limiting factor for the global vaccine supply. He is even thinking of granting licenses to selected producers. His Moderna competitor Bancel takes a similar view. He does not want to sue other companies that use his patents during the coronavirus crisis, but will certainly grant licenses afterwards. The pharmaceutical industry, on the other hand, takes a different view: it sees vaccines more as a commodity. Han Steutel, President of the German Association of Research-Based Pharmaceutical Companies ( ), told Handelsblatt: ""The manufacturers of mRNA vaccines have done more than ten years of groundwork to be able to help the world now. Where are saving ideas supposed to come from in the next pandemic and who is supposed to finance their implementation until they are ready for production when everyone knows that the inventors' patents will be taken away anyway?"" Patent law experts take a similar view. Tim Reinhard, partner at the international commercial law firm Osborne Clarke, says: ""It is dangerous if pharmaceutical and biotech companies have to fear that the fruits of their research will be confiscated in the future and that they will be forced to disclose their research results without adequate compensation."" Patent lawyer Ralph Nack from the commercial law firm Noerr points out: ""However, we will also need courageous and well-funded investors in future crises, and they will rely in particular on patent protection when making their investment decisions."" Claudia Milbradt from the law firm Clifford Chance sees yet another possibility to remedy the vaccine shortage through state intervention. It is calling for an obligation to hand over the raw materials, but the Americans are currently refusing to do so - as can be seen from the example of India. This could at least remedy the lack of raw material supplies for vaccines. According to the Chatham House think tank, there is also a lack of glass vials, bioreactor bags for cell cultures, fetal calf serum as a medium for cell cultures and nanoparticles in which some vaccines have to be stored in order to increase production capacity. The problem of how long the high demand will continue to determine the price will not last much longer anyway, as the established coronavirus vaccine manufacturers are pursuing gigantic production plans: BioNTech and Pfizer together are planning to produce around 2.5 billion doses in 2021 and Moderna wants to produce up to one billion units.

Supply Chain Act: The question of liability The German government has been at odds over the Supply Chain Act for months. It is intended to oblige German companies to comply with human rights due diligence obligations with their suppliers around the world. The biggest point of contention is the question of companies' liability if they violate these duties of care. Employment Minister Hubertus Heil (SPD) and Development Aid Minister Gerd Müller (CSU) are in favor of a liability mechanism and have the backing of civil society, trade unions and churches. Economics Minister Peter Altmaier (CDU) is against this, as are the leading German business associations. However, there are also companies and associations that are in principle in favor of liability. The European brand association AIM, which represents around 2,500 companies such as Beiersdorf, Nestlé and Puma, stated with regard to a European supply chain law: companies should be able to be held liable for not having established and applied sufficient due diligence procedures. The three ministries want to try again this week to resolve the dispute over the issue. It is necessary to finally talk about what liability could look like in order to find a compromise, says Cornelia Heydenreich from the Supply Chain Act Initiative. In fact, the impression that only a supply chain law provides a liability basis for lawsuits is wrong. In fact, Section 823 of the German Civil Code already provides such a basis for liability, which generally applies to all companies, whether large or small. However, Ministers Heil and Müller actually want to define civil liability more precisely in a supply chain law and thus simplify the legal options for those affected. This is what the original but unpublished key points of the law envisage. Companies could protect themselves - without solving a problem. Even companies that are generally committed to a supply chain law with enforcement mechanisms have their doubts about the usefulness of civil liability. There is a danger that companies will then act in such a way ""that they are as well protected as possible against lawsuits"", said Tchibo manager Nanda Bergstein last week at a hearing in the Bundestag's Human Rights Committee. Companies could, for example, rely on private auditing companies to check suppliers. In the past, problems have not been solved in this way. ""In the worst case, there are even incentives to conceal the actual conditions so that they are not held accountable,"" said Bergstein. In contrast, the human rights organization ECCHR, which has supported lawsuits against KiK or TÜV Süd in German courts, considers civil liability in the Supply Chain Act to be indispensable. Liability for injury to life, limb, property and other rights within the meaning of Section 823 of the German Civil Code (BGB) is not sufficient, said lawyer Miriam Saage-Maaß at the hearing: ""What is needed is an expansion of the protected goods to include the recognized catalog of human rights."" Nevertheless, a compromise by the German government could include waiving extended civil liability within a supply chain law. If companies fail to comply with due diligence obligations, fines of up to ten percent of turnover could be imposed and the company could be excluded from public procurement procedures or foreign trade promotion. With strong enforcement by the authorities, the focus would be on prevention, i.e. preventing damage from occurring in the first place. However, some of those involved wonder whether an authority could fulfill this task effectively. Those in favor of a compromise believe that the creation of a supply chain law alone will make it easier for those affected to take legal action. However, according to negotiating circles, it was previously considered a red line of the SPD to waive civil liability in the Supply Chain Act. Christian Socialist Development Minister Gerd Müller is considered more flexible on this point. He is primarily concerned with the introduction of a regulation for supply chains. So far, Economics Minister Altmaier has made little progress on the issue of liability.

German companies in Russia: Square, practical, angry German companies in Russia Square, practical, angry. German companies such as Ritter Sport are still active in war-torn Russia. There are many reasons for this. For weeks, companies that continue to do business in Russia have been harshly criticized. The Ukrainian ambassador to Germany, Andrij Melnyk, shared a picture on Twitter of a bar of Ritter Sport chocolate and a variation of its slogan - ""Square. Practical. Blood."" - because the company continues to sell chocolate in Russian supermarkets. In the weeks following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, some companies, including VW, Continental and Obi, shut down their operations. However, many companies have decided to remain in Russia for the time being. It is not known how many of the approximately 3,500 German companies that still existed at the beginning of the war have since frozen their production or left the country altogether. Both large companies and medium-sized enterprises for which Russia is a large sales market, such as the machine manufacturers Liebherr and Grimme, the Globus supermarket chain and Ritter Sport, have remained. The chocolate manufacturer's main reason for remaining in its second most important market is that it would have to discontinue some of its production in Germany and Austria and its cooperation with cocoa farmers and their collectives if they withdrew. They promise to donate all their profits from Russia to aid organizations and have already stopped all investments and advertising measures. Whether the company makes profits transparent and to which organizations donations are made was not disclosed to taz. Henkel also stated that it had stopped all investment, sponsorship and advertising expenditure and was only producing and supplying ""everyday goods"" such as cleaning agents. Like most companies, Henkel defends its decision by saying it has a responsibility to its employees. The Russian government had threatened executives of companies that had left the country with legal consequences. However, no such cases are known to date. Companies fear being expropriated. The reluctance of companies is also due to the fact that a law is being prepared in Russia with the help of which foreign companies can be expropriated if they withdraw from the Russian market, even temporarily. The law is intended to secure jobs and production capacities. This would make a return after the war very expensive at the very least. Pharmaceutical companies such as Bayer and Fresenius in particular also argue that they sell essential medicines and services. Fresenius operates more than 100 dialysis centers for kidney and liver patients. At the request of the taz, Bayer writes that it will only continue to sell ""indispensable"" products, but would not comment on the criteria it uses to select these and whether, for example, the headache tablet Aspirin is also meant. In addition to medical products, Bayer also supplies seeds to Russian farmers. ""Depriving the civilian population of essential health and agricultural products would only multiply the death toll of this war,"" they wrote in a statement. Food wholesaler Metro, which generates 240 million euros, or ten percent of its turnover, in Russia, also argues that it is supplying the Russian population. According to its own information, it mainly supplies restaurants, intermediaries and caterers - so it is questionable whether the loss of its 93 markets would jeopardize the food supply. Apart from their symbolic value, the financial consequences of German companies leaving the country would be manageable for the Russian state treasury in most cases. The sales, income and capital gains taxes of all Russian companies and individuals account for less than 10 percent of annual revenues.

Despite weak sales figures, Tesla surprises with profit and is worth more than GM Tesla surprisingly returned to profit in the third quarter, sending the US electric car manufacturer's share price soaring along with good news from China. After two quarters in the red, the company posted a profit of 143 million dollars (128.6 million euros) between July and September. Analysts had expected the worst in view of the recent weak sales figures for the vehicles and had assumed a loss. Tesla's turnover in the third quarter amounted to 5.4 billion dollars. The car manufacturer's share price rose by over 20 percent in electronic after-hours trading. US investors' delight at this quarterly profit made Elon Musk's company the most valuable American car manufacturer on Thursday. Tesla shares rose by 17 percent on Wall Street to 298 dollars (268 euros), giving them a market capitalization of 53 billion dollars. The electric car manufacturer thus overtook the long-established company General Motors (GM), which has 51 billion dollars. Delivery target remains. Investors thus also acknowledged statements by company boss Elon Musk, who expressed ""complete confidence"" that the annual delivery target of 360,000 to 400,000 new cars could still be achieved. Tesla has recently managed to significantly reduce its costs, which is why it has returned to profitability, the company announced. Tesla also announced the start of production on a trial basis at its new factory in China. The so-called Gigafactory in Shanghai was built in just ten months and is now ""ready for production"". The factory is expected to reach an annual capacity of 500,000 cars. Tesla hopes that this will give it a significant boost in production and direct access to the dynamic Chinese market for electric vehicles. Focus on energy sector. The difficulties in meeting demand have long been a problem for the US company. Last year in particular, Tesla had to repeatedly adjust the production target it had set itself. The company is now confident that it will remain profitable throughout the second half of the year. The company also referred to other areas outside of electric car production: Tesla has needed all its resources for the Model 3 for the past two years, Musk said. Now sales of this model, which is so important for the company, have increased by 50 percent in the past quarter compared to the previous year and the pressure is easing. Tesla can therefore now focus more on the energy sector again, Musk said. The company also manufactures solar panels and electricity storage solutions.

A municipality wants to become ""energy self-sufficient"": How can Iffeldorf get rid of oil and gas? Iffeldorf is not in a particularly good position when it comes to renewable energies. Their share of electricity and heat is only 17 and 18 percent respectively. The citizens' meeting now focused on how the municipality can get rid of oil and natural gas. Solar systems, groundwater pumps and district heating islands were discussed, as well as wind power. Iffeldorf - Around 270 people came to the citizens' meeting in the Iffeldorf community center, far more than a few days earlier in Penzberg. The main topic was the energy transition. Mayor Hans Lang (SPD) had announced in advance that it was ""about our path to becoming an energy self-sufficient village"" based on renewable energies. In Iffeldorf, their share is currently 30 percent below the national average and 35 percent below the state average. According to Lang, the majority of energy, namely 85 percent, is used for heating and hot water in Iffeldorf. The invited speaker was Andreas Scharli from ""Energiewende Oberland"", which aims to make the four participating districts independent of fossil fuels by 2035. He began by making it clear that this goal could not be achieved without making savings, for example with the help of building insulation or control technology. As a quick measure, Scharli recommended lowering the hot water temperature and the heating limit temperature on the boiler. ""There is a lot of potential."" Groundwater heat pumps and district solutions for local heating. Scharli also had some special advice for Iffeldorf. Groundwater heat pumps could work well ""because the groundwater is not far away here,"" he said. The energy consultant considers a district heating network with a central heating plant like the one in Penzberg to be impractical for Iffeldorf due to the costs and high heat losses over long distances. However, Scharli believes it is conceivable to supply individual areas or residential districts, i.e. to rely on neighborhood solutions. According to him, so-called ""cold local heating"" could be an option, in which water at a temperature of ten to twelve degrees is transported into the building via a network of pipes to a heat pump. This could also be used for cooling in summer. Photovoltaics: ""There are still enough roofs available in Iffeldorf"" Scharli also promoted photovoltaics. ""There are still enough roofs available in Iffeldorf,"" he said and recommended taking a look at the district's solar register. According to him, solar systems on south-facing facades are also a possibility. ""It works extremely well in winter."" Perhaps there is also a corner for an open-air facility in Iffeldorf, said Scharli. Mayor Lang confirmed that an area was urgently needed. According to him, a solar park could be operated by an energy cooperative in which the population is involved. Question about wind power potential in Iffeldorf. The subsequent discussion was very lively. For example, questions were asked about the wind power potential, which, according to Scharli's assessment, is ""not very high"", especially as it would also need an investor who ultimately wants to earn money. One Iffeldorfer recommended taking a closer look at the wind atlas because of an area near the highway. Regarding wind power, Mayor Lang explained that there is the possibility of participating in a wind turbine in another region, for example in the Allgäu, through a cooperative that is yet to be founded. One question at the citizens' meeting was what the municipality meant by ""energy self-sufficiency"". Scharli and Lang explained that the aim was to achieve ""balance sheet self-sufficiency"". This means that the municipality generates as much energy over the year as it consumes during this period, which is not true self-sufficiency. Mayor has high hopes for the new ""Energy Working Group"" The mayor also addressed energy issues in his report. He reported that a PV system had been installed on the roof of the children's house, that the building yard now had an electric car and that a second one was about to be delivered. The plan is to install four e-charging points in 2023. There are also plans to offer a car for e-car sharing. In response to the suggestion that street lamps should be switched off at night, Lang said that all 250 lamps had already been converted to LED and that a good 70 percent of them could be dimmed. He also has high hopes for the new ""Energy Working Group"", which consists of 14 people. He hopes that the working group will one day also be able to advise private individuals, especially in times when energy consultants are so busy that it is almost impossible to get an appointment.

Höhle der Löwen: Ankerkraut deal with Nestlé causes a disastrous response - ""Soul sold to the devil"" Nestlé acquires a majority stake in the Hamburg-based spice manufacturer Ankerkraut. But customers and cooperation partners are not at all enthusiastic about this. On Wednesday, the spice company Ankerkraut announced that the food group Nestlé is now the majority shareholder. While the founders describe this move as ""a great opportunity"", the deal has largely fallen flat with most observers and fans. On social media platforms such as Twitter and Instagram, many users are not happy about the ""Lion's Den"" start-up's deal. And even on the job platform LinkedIn, which is otherwise known for its predominantly positive comments, the deal has been met with unusually harsh criticism. The comments under the company's announcement post are clear. ""You have sold your soul to the devil"", ""When greed eats the brain - never ever more Ankerkraut in my kitchen"" or ""Unfortunately, I took a wrong turn and hit the wall with momentum"" are just a few of the hundreds of comments from disappointed customers. But consumers are not the only ones who are disappointed. A major cooperation partner has also made it clear in a public statement what it thinks of the news. YouTube star LeFloid, who regularly inspires several million subscribers with his videos, actually had a cooperation with Ankerkraut. But since the Nestle deal, this is now history. On Instagram, he writes: ""Since a cooperation with Nestlé is out of the question for us, we see no other option than to end the cooperation with Ankerkraut as soon as possible."" LeFloid receives a lot of encouragement from his fans. One user writes: ""The right decision. Too bad about the store, but there are certainly alternatives with more backbone."" Another says: ""Hats off to this decision. I personally think it's absolutely right and exemplary of you, especially given the 'scope' of the decision for you."" In fact, LeFloid had even launched his own spice called ""Holy Smokes"" with Ankerkraut. It is not yet known what will happen with the YouTuber's spice mix. But why do so many consumers resist the food giant Nestlé? The company gained its dubious reputation through numerous scandals. Former Nestle Chairman of the Board of Directors Peter Brabeck-Letmathe probably caused the greatest damage to the company's image in an interview in 2005. At that time, he spoke about water and explained that this raw material has a market value and is therefore not a public good. Most of the audience concluded from this that Brabeck-Letmathe did not see water as a human right. On its website, however, the company backtracks: ""At Nestlé, we firmly believe that access to water is a fundamental human right. We fully recognize the human right to water, which was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 2010."" Regarding the interview in question, it says: ""The interview in the video is an excerpt from a documentary from 2005 that has been taken out of context. This excerpt misrepresents the view of our Chairman Emeritus. He has repeatedly said that all people have the right to clean water to meet their hydration and basic hygiene needs."" Nestlé is also heavily criticized for buying water rights. The problem: where Nestlé taps the water, it becomes a scarce commodity. This is a major problem in the French village of Vittel* . The groundwater level continues to fall - the villagers protest. In addition, there are further scandals involving milk powder for babies, criticism of the excessive sugar content in the products and the mountains of waste generated by Nespresso coffee capsules. So there are many reasons why consumers may decide not to buy Nestlé products. The bad reputation of the large corporation is now also becoming the undoing of the originally small start-up Ankerkraut.

Study: Bitcoin environment changed massively in 2021 2021 was not only characterized by extreme price movements in the crypto sector, but also by important events - including China's ban on Bitcoin mining and the introduction of Bitcoin as a means of payment in El Salvador. In its ""Crypto Outlook 2022"", crypto service provider Bitcoin Suisse is convinced that these events will have far-reaching consequences - both this year and in the years to come. The exodus of Bitcoin miners from China has clear geopolitical implications, as Bitcoin Suisse Head of Research Markus Dapp emphasized on Friday at the presentation of the new report. After China took itself out of the game, the USA now provides over a third of the computing power for validating Bitcoin transactions. Mining activities have also increased significantly in Kazakhstan, Russia and Canada. However, an even broader diversification would certainly be desirable, admitted Dapp. Bitcoin official means of payment in first country The adoption of Bitcoin by a first country is also likely to have been of geopolitical significance. With this step, El Salvador in Central America has gone against the explicit recommendations of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, Bitcoin Suisse recalls. It remains to be seen whether other countries will join in the current year. El Salvador's move has also put the spotlight on Lightning technology, which is based on the Bitcoin network and enables fast and cheap Bitcoin transactions. The inhabitants of El Salvador, 70 percent of whom have no bank account, would now have a safe and cheap way to receive vital foreign remittances. Dapp also pointed out that criminals in El Salvador had specialized directly in robbing people as they left money transfer offices such as ""Western Union"". For the crypto expert, the positive social contribution of Bitcoin is generally underestimated in the discussion about its ESG impact. For countries with functioning banking systems such as Switzerland or Western Europe, this is likely to play less of a role, Dapp conceded. However, the low entry threshold to the Bitcoin system could change life for the 1.7 billion unbanked people worldwide. Experts put Bitcoin's energy requirements into perspective Bitcoin Suisse economists also put the accusations that cryptocurrencies are highly damaging to the environment into perspective. They consider the frequent comparisons of Bitcoin's energy consumption with that of a country such as Argentina to make little sense. According to estimates, Bitcoin consumes 188 terawatt hours (TWh) of global energy production per year, which is around 0.12 percent - less than gold production (571 TWh), computer games (214 TWh) or annual Christmas lighting (201 TWh), for example. Ethereum faces ""open-heart surgery"" Meanwhile, the second most important cryptocurrency, Ethereum, has an important year ahead of it, as its ""smart contract"" blockchain has seen an explosion of applications in areas such as DeFi (decentralized finance) and NFTs (non-fungible tokens) in the past year. At the same time, the Ethereum ecosystem is in strong competition with fast-growing and extremely ""agile"" competitors such as Solana, Cardano and Polkadot. Ethereum is now about to take the next technical step towards the much more complex ""Ethereum 2.0"" this year, which includes switching to the much less energy-intensive ""Proof of Stake"" process. The complex undertaking is like ""open heart surgery"", said Dapp - the chances of success are around 50:50. Meanwhile, Ethereum's competitors are not sleeping: ""If there are delays, the competition will continue to grow.""

The transformation of Bitcoin - We are living through a monetary revolution - and Bitcoin is on the road to victory One should be careful with these words - too often they have been punished dearly on the stock market. But with Bitcoin, everything could really be different this time. Because something has fundamentally changed. During the first Bitcoin hype, the dream was that the cryptocurrency really could one day replace the euro. There were also many small private investors in the market. But this time, investing in Bitcoin is about something else: ""We are living through a currency revolution so multifaceted that few of us realize its full extent,"" wrote economic historian Niall Ferguson in a recent guest article. ""The technological transformation of the Internet is driving this revolution. The 2020 pandemic has accelerated it."" Bitcoin has more than doubled in 2020 - and the prospects for a further rise are good. Find out from Bitcoin expert Jörg Hermsdorf on December 8 what the drivers of the rally are and how best to invest in Bitcoin. Click HERE to register! In view of the growing money supply, investors are trying to protect their assets against possible inflation. Distrust of paper currencies is growing. In the past, money flowed into real estate, shares and gold during such phases. It is doing so again - only now some of the assets are also going into Bitcoin. ""This rally is being driven by smart and institutional money and is not built on speculation alone,"" said Guy Hirsch, managing director for the U.S. at eToro. ""Many individuals and asset managers are now buying in."" Bitcoin could take the place of gold. Bitcoin is also scarce and cannot be multiplied at will - two fundamental characteristics that asset protection needs. Bitcoin offers built-in scarcity in a virtual world characterized by limitless abundance. ""Do I believe that bitcoin is a permanent fixture that could largely take the place of gold? Yes, I do, because it's so much more functional than passing around a gold bar,"" said Rick Rieder, chief fixed income strategist at Blackrock, the world's largest asset manager, recently. If this thesis proves true, then the rise of Bitcoin is far from over: ""If the world's millionaires shift just one percent of their assets into Bitcoin, the price will rise to 75,000 dollars,"" calculates Ferguson in his guest article. ""It may even rise higher if you consider that many bitcoins have disappeared."" However, it is also clear that the further establishment of Bitcoin will not be a one-way street. There will be setbacks and bumpy passages. It is therefore important to invest with caution and prudence. Because even if many things change, some things remain the same.

Surveillance with Apple Airtags: Apple, listen to the signals Data protectionists can warn about security gaps as often as they like. They are rarely heard by the companies. Airtags are designed to make the annoying search for or loss of keys or wallets a thing of the past Privacy advocates like Lothar Wieler and Christian Drosten have been feeling the same way for years. They warn, repeat themselves, provide evidence for their warnings and repeat themselves. And when case XY occurs, nobody wants to have known anything about it. The story of the new Airtags added to the Apple range in the summer can be summarized in a similar way. Stories of misuse are now piling up. The airtags, which are about the size of a 2-euro coin, are designed to make searching for or losing keys or wallets a thing of the past. The standard version of the Apple Airtag costs 35 euros. Apple has also thought of design lovers: Airtags are available in the exclusive Hermès version, from 300 euros upwards. The waterproof air tag contains a U1 chip with ultra-wideband technology that can be tracked via Bluetooth. Apple has of course not invented a new product with this; location tags have been around for a long time from various companies. Apple has improved the proximity search in particular to get an even more precise location. In addition, owners can now send a message to potential finders. Basically, all locating tags work according to the same principle: at regular intervals, they send out an identifier via Bluetooth that can be used to identify them. If a nearby smartphone receives the transmission, it links the data with its own current position and forwards it to the manufacturer. And now comes the Apple twist: While other manufacturers rely on as many users as possible downloading their app in order to get enough data, Apple has integrated the function directly into iOS: Every Apple mobile device that has the ""Where is? "" app forwards the airtags to Apple. This function is activated by default on all Apple mobile devices. Instructions for espionage. Apple asserted that it had considered everything when it came to data protection. There are now videos on Tiktok in which people discover foreign airtags on their cars, for example. Others explain how best to use the tags for spying - from a quick microphone removal to the perfect hiding place. Although the tags constantly change their Bluetooth Mac address and encrypt their data, only the owner can then identify them. It is practically impossible to identify the perpetrators. A warning signal, which is intended to draw attention to secret tracking, only sounds when the tag has been out of reach of its owner for three days. However, if the airtag reappears in the vicinity of its owner, the warning does not appear. The warning signals to Apple did not fail to materialize back then, and now they are getting louder again. Perhaps the company is simply trying to ride out the second wave of outrage.

Can the coronavirus be eradicated? Researchers present mathematical model Theoretically, the global eradication of Covid-19 would be possible, as the study in the journal BMJ Global Health states According to the researchers, eradicating Covid-19 would be even easier than eradicating polio, but more difficult than eradicating smallpox. Success depends on various factors - technical, socio-political and economic. Eradicating Covid-19 - researchers answer this important question. ""The analysis shows that the eradication of Covid-19 is within the realms of technical feasibility,"" said Professor Nick Wilson from the University of Otago and author of the study in a press release. In his opinion, the combination of vaccination programs, public health measures and global interest in combating the disease are helping to make eradication possible. The scientists used a complex mathematical model to evaluate the eradication of three diseases - Covid-19, polio and smallpox. 17 variables - including the availability of a safe and effective vaccine, the possibility of lifelong immunity, public health measures and infection control - were taken into account in the model. Smallpox, which was declared eradicated in 1980, received the highest average score for the feasibility of eradication, according to the scientists. On a three-point scale with the 17 variables, smallpox was rated with an average of 2.7. In comparison, Covid-19 had an average score of 1.6 and polio an average score of 1.5. Coronavirus: eradication of Covid-19 possible according to researchers Vaccination programs were largely responsible for the worldwide eradication of smallpox, the researchers explain. In the case of Covid-19, a combination of vaccination programs, public health measures and global interest in combating the disease could help to eradicate the coronavirus. Some parts of the world - New Zealand, for example - have been ""corona-free"" for a long period of time without vaccinations. According to Wilson, this already points to a technical possibility of eradicating Covid-19 worldwide. In order to defeat Covid-19, Prof. Wilson to rely on so-called ring vaccination programs, as in the fight against smallpox. These programs were aimed primarily at the contact persons of the infected persons and thus ensured the eradication of smallpox. Herd immunity was therefore not necessary. According to the scientists, the biggest challenges would be to achieve a high vaccination coverage rate against Sars-CoV2 and to adapt the vaccine to the corona mutations. According to the researchers, the acceptance of the coronavirus vaccine is low compared to smallpox and polio. A vaccination quota necessary for eradication would fail in many rich countries due to vaccination refusals. In poorer countries, on the other hand, there are still too few vaccines to achieve the necessary vaccination rates. The scientists are calling for close international cooperation in the face of ""vaccine nationalism"" and ""anti-science movements"". Wilson and his team point out that their analysis still needs to be peer-reviewed. An investigation into the benefits and costs of eradicating Covid-19 is also necessary. Moreover, it is important to distinguish between eradicating a disease and reducing the infection rate in a particular geographical region. Polio and smallpox. Polio - poliomyelitis - polio. There have been no cases of polio (infantile paralysis) in Germany for many years. But the virus has still not been eradicated. There is still a risk of contracting polio abroad. Vaccination against polio is therefore important. Smallpox - leaf blisters, called Variola major, Variola vera or smallpox. Smallpox has been officially eradicated since the 1980s. Global vaccination programs have been terminated. Only two WHO reference laboratories in the USA and Russia still have smallpox strains, according to the Robert Koch Institute (RKI). For centuries there were repeated outbreaks of smallpox, and in the 18th century, the disease was spread to the whole country. In the 20th century, 400,000 people in Europe died from it every year.

Denmark | Elections in Denmark: Narrow majority for left-wing alliance The left-wing alliance around Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen's Social Democrats has won the parliamentary elections. According to the final result published on Wednesday night, Frederiksen's red bloc won a total of 90 out of 179 seats in the Danish parliament - and thus a narrow government majority. After the result was announced, Frederiksen announced the formal resignation of her government and coalition negotiations for a broad coalition for Wednesday. Frederiksen's red bloc won 87 seats, plus three seats in Greenland and on the Faroe Islands. The alliance of liberals, conservatives and right-wing populists, known as the blue bloc, won a total of 73 seats in the elections. Former Prime Minister Lars Lökke Rasmussen's Moderate Party enters parliament for the first time with 16 MPs. Frederiksen's Social Democrats are the clear winners of the election: 27.5 percent of voters voted for the party, giving it 50 seats in the parliament in Copenhagen. Compared to the 2019 election, the party gained 1.6 percentage points. Opinion polls, on the other hand, had pointed to a historically poor result for the Social Democrats, while the post-election surveys published on Tuesday evening suggested that neither of the two blocs had achieved a majority. On Wednesday, Prime Minister Frederiksen spoke of the Social Democrats' best result for over 20 years and held out the prospect of coalition negotiations starting soon. When the Social Democrats say something, we stick to it,"" said the 44-year-old, referring to her proposal during the election campaign to lead a cross-party government alliance. The Social Democrats are a party for the whole of Denmark. In addition to the fight against inflation, the main topics in the election campaign were climate issues and healthcare policy. On Sunday, around 50,000 people, including Frederiksen, took part in a climate march through Copenhagen. Immigration did not play a role; in the EU country, there has been cross-party agreement on a restrictive immigration policy for a good 20 years. Frederiksen has embodied the new course of the Danish Social Democrats since taking office as head of government. The party combines a restrictive immigration policy with the promise to protect the welfare state. Frederiksen's overall management of the country during the coronavirus pandemic was praised, but the 44-year-old prime minister has been dogged by the mink scandal for some time: in the wake of the coronavirus pandemic, her government ordered the killing of all 15 million farmed mink in the country in November 2020. The aim was to prevent the spread of a mutated form of Sars-CoV-2 that could be transmitted to humans and was feared to impair the effectiveness of future vaccines. As it turned out later, there was no legal basis for the measure; it was only created after the fact. Both left-wing and right-wing parties then called for new elections. The next parliamentary elections were not actually due to take place until June 2023.

PNP interview: Hofreiter: ""Shameful that politics is failing in climate protection"" Anton Hofreiter, parliamentary party leader of the Greens, criticizes the German government's environmental policy as ""shameful"" in an interview with the PNP. ""It is shameful that politicians are failing to protect the climate and are not taking the necessary measures to ensure that young people have a secure future,"" says Hofreiter about the ""Fridays for Future"" movement, in which tens of thousands of schoolchildren demonstrate week after week for climate protection. It is telling that pupils now have to fight to ensure that their own livelihoods are not destroyed. When young people's commitment and protests for their own future ""are then criticized and dismissed by politicians, as the FDP does, I lack any understanding for it"". ""50,000 e-cars - that's an indictment of poverty"" Hofreiter has a bad opinion of the ""Concerted Action on Mobility"" planned by the coalition committee. Above all, ""more meetings with the bosses of the automotive industry are planned. This has little to do with a ""concerted action on mobility"","" the Green politician pointed out, noting that the Federal Minister of Transport had met the car bosses 15 times last year, but not at all with the environmental associations. ""This clearly shows that there is a need to catch up on climate and environmental protection, not the corporate bosses."" The Merkel government had set the target of putting one million electric cars on the roads by 2020, Hofreiter recalled, referring to the intentions to promote e-mobility. ""In 2019, we are only at 50,000. That is an indictment."" On the climate cabinet: ""You don't need a working group"" On the climate cabinet that the coalition committee wants to set up, Hofreiter said: ""Nobody would be happier than me if the federal government finally protected the climate. But the Grand Coalition works according to the motto, if you don't know what to do, set up a working group. In order to make progress on climate protection, the expansion of renewable energies must be driven forward again. ""Wind power slumped by half last year. Something has to happen here. You don't need a working group for that."" ""The Bavarian state government has systematically ensured that the Free State is left behind when it comes to wind power"" According to Hofreiter, the fact that consumers have to pay such high electricity prices is due to the exemptions and subsidies for the industry. He believes that another reason why cheap wind power, for example, is not reaching Bavaria is the Bavarian state government, which has long delayed and blocked the expansion of power lines and the grid. Hofreiter complains: ""The state government has systematically ensured that the Free State is being left behind here. It sabotaged the expansion of wind power and fought against every single wind turbine that the municipalities wanted to build.""

The next president: How Joe Biden defeated Donald Trump It is not known how many of the 3,500 court cases that Donald Trump has conducted directly or indirectly during his lifetime have ended favorably for him. As far as the legal rearguard action with which America's president wants to turn the defeat around five minutes after 12 is concerned, a preliminary figure has already been set: towards zero. All attempts by the Trump campaign to have the election results qualified as fraudulent by the competent courts of the states concerned have so far failed. In Michigan, Trump wanted to stop the counting of ballots until his own election observers were allowed to supervise the procedure - judges rejected this as unfounded. Moreover, the result was already clear: Biden. In Wisconsin, Trump claimed voting was hindered by queues and faulty voting machines and demanded a recount - rejected. In Georgia, Trump cited a poll worker who claimed to have observed that 53 ballots arrived late and were counted - rejected. Because ""hearsay"", according to the judge. In Nevada, Trump's former ambassador to Germany, Richard Grenell, went on the record and announced a lawsuit because several thousand people had allegedly voted illegally. Asked by journalists for evidence, Grenell fled into a bus. Later, state election officials declared that it is legitimate to vote in Nevada even if you don't live there. In Detroit, Trump filed a lawsuit because Republican election observers had been denied access during the count - in the judicial hearing, it embarrassingly turned out that 100 observers from both parties were present. The judge rolls his eyes. Renowned constitutional lawyers make it clear on US television that Trump has so far only made allegations garnished with imprecise terms such as ""irregularities"" and ""lack of transparency"", which no court will be impressed by. On the contrary. The more often Trump talks about a ""stolen"" election, the less judges would ""take it seriously"", said law professor Jonathan Turley, who is sympathetic to Trump. Ben Ginsberg, who spent many years as a lawyer for the Republicans, speaks of ""Hail Mary"" lawsuits, in reference to a play in American football that is supposed to turn around a game that is already as good as lost at the last minute. As recently as Friday, Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito ruled that absentee ballots received by the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals in Pennsylvania could not be used. The votes received before 8 p.m. on November 3 and bearing the postmark 3.11. must be counted and stored separately. But: Alito deliberately rejected the Trump camp's demand to declare these votes invalid now. Local election officials signaled that the order of the highest court would not have any major consequences. Timothy O'Brien, once Trump's biographer and (unsuccessfully) sued by the New York businessman in 2006, sees Trump's legal smokescreens as an attempt to knit a stab-in-the-back legend. This is intended to suppress the ""loser image"" (the first president in almost 30 years not to get a second term in office) in the public eye. Hundreds of Trump fans have already bitten the bullet and are demonstrating for their president. According to O'Brien, America can expect a long-term Trump narrative that starts something like this: If I hadn't been cheated in the 2020 election...

Culture ""Verbal artillery"": Andrij Melnyk defends his PR tactics He is once again present on all channels, which is highly remarkable for a Deputy Foreign Minister. But Andrij Melnyk (47), Ukraine's ambassador to Germany until October last year, apparently enjoys public attention more than almost any other diplomat and even welcomes criticism. The ""Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung"", for example, wrote about him under the commentary heading ""Noise instead of debate"" that he had strongly influenced German Russia policy with his demands ""from the outside"": ""The former Ukrainian ambassador was a master at this, he once blamed Germany for many deaths in his country due to a lack of arms deliveries."" ""They think that's it"" Melnyk tweeted his thanks for this editorial, which he described as a ""compliment"", and replied: ""Without this noise, there would never have been a debate about arms deliveries in Germany."" At the same time, he tried to put further pressure on Federal Chancellor Olaf Scholz. The Germans ""leaned back too soon"", the diplomat said in a recent interview with the Ukrainian portal NV: ""They think, well, that's it, it was a difficult birth, to put it that way, it took more than nine months, these tank births took almost a year, and now it turns out that you can breathe out, relax and put your feet up, we shouldn't expect anything else."" However, this was ""wrong"", said Melnyk, adding that Ukraine could expect ""larger quantities"" of weapons from Germany: ""I know that they are available."" In a tweet, the Deputy Foreign Minister assured that he was not constantly demanding more weapons from his allies ""just for fun"", but was determined to initiate debates, even if he did not achieve his goals ""tomorrow"" and was sometimes subjected to scorn and ridicule. In a further interview with the public television station in Ukraine, Melnyk now explained in detail why he is so present in the media: ""This is a forced step. We are all well-mannered, polite and no one has given up on classic diplomacy. But the war came to our country. Germany is the fourth largest economy in the world. A country that is one of the top 5 arms exporters. The Germans exported weapons worth nine billion euros in the year before the war. Then they tell us that they can supply 5,000 helmets, and that's after long discussions."" ""It was a cry for help"" He is ""not sure"" whether he will maintain his sometimes polemical style of communication. He described his tweets as an ""experiment that was and is fraught with risk"". He is fully aware that he has outraged some people in Germany, but the results are more important than taking this into account: ""In this situation, it seemed less risky to go on the offensive."" The ex-ambassador compared himself to a drowning man searching for a lifebuoy: ""I regret and regret that I had to use such heavy verbal artillery, but in hindsight it was the only possible method. The point is not that any politician there might feel attacked, but that German society understands: If the Ukrainians are using such methods, then the situation there is pretty bad. It was a cry for help,"" says Melnyk. ""They call it coordination"" In peacetime, an ambassador usually has no access to Federal Chancellor Olaf Scholz. The usual official business would be handled at the level of state secretaries. This made his Twitter messages all the more important: ""I knew that every message I sent would be read by Scholz's office manager within a second. This is [Chancellery Minister] Wolfgang Schmidt. I know he won't like it, that he'll probably let out a few quiet or even loud curses, but I also know that the message will arrive in a matter of seconds and within an hour someone will comment on it and there will already be a discussion."" Incidentally, Melnyk says that he is currently no longer responsible for Germany, but for Latin America, the USA and Canada. But even in this role, he wants to influence political Berlin, because Germany often orients itself towards allies: ""They call it coordination. This means that we can use these levers both via Latin America and via the United States to promote some processes in Europe."" ""Russia must be de-Nazified"" Asked how he envisioned a ""victory"" for Ukraine, Melnyk replied: ""Russia must go through what the Germans went through on 8 September. May 1945. Not only complete and unconditional surrender without [prior] negotiations, because nobody negotiated with Hitler either, although he had tried in the last few months. But what happened after that? Germany was occupied by the Allies and there was a process of so-called denazification, which the Russians wanted to carry out in our country.""
