However, because we as legislators are responsible for spending tens of billions of American taxpayer dollars for military support in this conflict, we believe that such participation in this war also carries with it a responsibility for the U.S. to seriously explore all possible ways, including direct contact with Russia, to limit the damage and support Ukraine in reaching a peaceful solution.... In conclusion, we call on you to engage in energetic diplomatic efforts in support of a negotiated solution and a ceasefire, to engage in direct talks with Russia, to sound out the prospects for a new, mutually acceptable European security agreement that would allow for a sovereign and independent Ukraine, and to work, in concert with our Ukrainian partners, to work for a swift end to the conflict and to affirm this goal as America's highest priority.

CDA wants to strengthen ties with Al Assad, but House rejects proposal CDA MP Martijn van Helvert wants the Netherlands to strengthen diplomatic ties with Syrian President Bashar Al Assad. According to Van Helvert, this is necessary to find a solution for the trial of Dutch IS fighters and the return of Syrians who fled Al Assad's regime. The Christian party made the proposal Wednesday in a debate in the House of Representatives, but found little support from both the opposition and coalition parties. ""Talking to Al Assad could be seen as losing political face,"" Van Helvert said. At the same time, he sees that the Americans, European partners, but also Islamic State have failed to topple Al Assad and that the Syrian dictator is firmly back in the saddle. The CDA member estimates that a future of Syria with Al Assad will provide the stability needed to return Syrian refugees to the Netherlands, among other things. And with Iraq not seeing the trial of Dutch IS fighters currently detained in Syria, the option of them being tried in Syria must be held up. CDA receives criticism from opposition and coalition. The VVD does not understand why the Netherlands has to make ""a knee-jerk reaction"" toward Al Assad, and on its own to strengthen ties. In the past, the party has advocated engaging precisely with dictators, but restoring diplomatic ties with Al Assad is going too far for VVD MP Sven Koopmans. ""How can Al Assad, who has hundreds of thousands of civilian deaths on his conscience, contribute to stability? What stability?"" , Koopmans believes. D66's Sjoerd Sjoerdsma also sees nothing in the proposal. ""Al Assad is Islamic State in a neat suit. He is a foster father of IS."" Sjoerdsma points out that Al Assad contributed to the rise of IS by releasing radical jihadists from Syrian prisons. Leaving justice for the Dutch IS'ers to Al Assad is a bad plan, according to the D66'er, since the Syrian president has released IS'ers in the past. Green Left warns that Al Assad's strengthening of diplomatic ties will be seen as a reward for ""his disgusting behavior."" The Labour Party points out that Syrian refugees were actually fleeing Al Assad's reign of terror. Block does not want to tighten ties. Therefore, it does not look like the Cabinet will heed the CDA's call. Minister Stef Blok (Foreign Affairs) said this weekend in an interview with NU.nl that there is no future for Al Assad in Syria. Blok said he cannot rule out the possibility that the Dutch IS currently detained in Syria could fall into the hands of Al Assad, but that does not mean the Netherlands will restore diplomatic ties. ""I will not let Al Assad blackmail me into strengthening diplomatic ties. For Al Assad, there is no future in Syria. The crimes against humanity he has committed are SO terrible. He cannot stay,"" Blok said. CDA points to diplomatic ties with China. Van Helvert agrees with the Chamber that Al Assad is responsible for atrocities against his own people, but reiterates that Western allies have failed to depose him. Now that Al Assad is more firmly in the saddle with Russia's help, following the departure of the Americans and Turkey's invasion, Van Helvert believes the Netherlands should at least strengthen ties at the lowest diplomatic level. He also points out to his fellow MPs that the Netherlands maintains good ties with China at the very highest level, while the country commits human rights violations on a large scale, such as the oppression of the Uighurs.

No family caregiver remains The recruitment of potential family caregivers is declining. A seventy-something who needs help with grocery shopping or chores around the house can currently call on an average of four family members or friends. In twenty years that will be only two , according to research by the Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency. In areas where young people are moving away, such as East Groningen, Zeelandic Flanders and South Limburg, even fewer caregivers remain. There, the elderly have only one person ""at their disposal. It's a side effect of the aging population, according to the PBL's ""Concern for Jobs"" study. By 2040, the Netherlands will have as many as 2.6 million people over 75, twice as many as today. Because of this growth, seventies, eighties and nineties will soon have fewer fit people around them to help them. More people at the same time. MantelzorgNL, the advocacy organization for family caregivers, is already noticing that the pressure is increasing. ""Informal caregivers report caring for more people at the same time more often than before. Sometimes for two or three,"" said director Liesbeth Hoogendijk. ""If it has to be this way, I don't have to do it anymore,"" they increasingly say. And they regularly wonder if they can say 'no' to some tasks."" The risk of the dwindling group of informal caregivers is that the people who help are increasingly burdened, Hoogendijk says. Sometimes they even run into burnout. ""In exceptional cases, it derails. The caregiver then neglects the one he cares for or uses physical violence."" PBL researcher Femke Daalhuizen fears isolation of the elderly if not enough is invested in care. ""There will be more fall incidents. I then expect that the elderly will more often request emergency care or need to be admitted to a care facility. The healthcare costs previously cut are thus shifted elsewhere in the healthcare sector."" Professional settings. But the elderly who turn to professional care facilities are also at risk of being squeezed out, PBL points out. Because to assist all those needing help over 75 in 20 years, twice as many district nurses and home care workers will be needed, 700,000 to be exact. But the Ministry of Health already foresees a shortage of more than 100,000 healthcare professionals in the coming years. ""Already we need to think about how to deliver care without needing staff,"" says PBL researcher Femke Daalhuizen. Distressing, thinks Tineke Abma, professor of diversity and participation at the VU Medical Center. Back in 2012, the Council for Health and Society warned of a staff shortage in elder care due to the aging population. 'Drastic choices are inevitable,' the council admonished. Abma: ""Yet two years later, a cut in healthcare came on top of that."" A wrong choice, she thinks. ""Nursing homes closed their doors, staff were laid off, and the industry as a whole became unattractive to work in."" As a result, in the remaining nursing homes, care is now nearly substandard, Abma says. ""I hear from the care facilities that I am a supervisor of that they cannot guarantee the quality and safety of the elderly because of the shortage of staff."" Abma even sees a dichotomy emerging among the elderly. ""Those with ample scholarship choose a commercial care facility or a home health nurse. Those who cannot afford it continue to live at home for too long, at the risk of accidents. Or relies on a public institution that has a long waiting list and cannot guarantee sufficient quality of care. Older people, they are not just middle-class pensionados enjoying life to the fullest. They are also busy volunteers, babysitting moms and dads, and caregivers who struggle with stress, or even burnout. One in five family caregivers find themselves tight on money. Informal caregivers often fail financially, research shows. Family and government must step in,

comments Trump will have to face the consequences of his rhetoric The president of the United States ""can no longer afford inaction."" Warning words of Dec. 17, 2012, addressed at this site to then-President... The president of the United States ""can no longer afford inaction."" Warnings of Dec. 17, 2012, addressed at this site to then-President Barack Obama. The weekend before, Adam Lanza had shot and killed 20 children and six adults at his former elementary school Sandy Hook, Connecticut. America was in a state of shock. This was never to happen again. Barack Obama cried along with the nation and promised action. But ""Sandy Hook"" did not become a turning point; it became the beginning of an epidemic increase in mass shootings. In schools, at festivals, in malls. This past weekend, shootings in the US left 22 dead in El Paso, Texas, and 10 dead in Dayton, Ohio. Nowhere is the gap between the will of citizens and the actions of politicians as wide as on this issue. Americans call for measures to curb firearm violence. For example, following the 2018 Parkland school massacre, 92 percent of Americans wanted stricter controls on firearm buyers. It didn't. The American political system rewards opportunism and makes real change impossible. Leadership is urgently needed here. The influence of outside funders, such as the National Rifle Association, on Congressmen and other representatives of the people is too great. The debate over political campaign financing needs to be revisited. But Donald Trump's America has a second problem. Barack Obama fell short with his measures, but at least he tried to comfort and unite his people, as his predecessors did. President Donald Trump only increases the contradictions. He thus gives political backing to extremists, in a climate where it is easy to put one's money where one's mouth is. The gunman in El Paso had chosen this city on the border with Mexico to counter an ""invasion"" of ""millions"" of migrants, a manifesto attributed to him showed. He spoke of the ""cultural and ethnic replacement"" by migrants, accusing the American media of spreading ""fake news."" They are echoes of the message Trump persistently preaches. Trump called Mexican migrants ""rapists"" in 2016 and has only further sharpened his tone. Four Democratic Congressmen of color, three of whom were born in the US, were advised to go back to their home countries if they do not like it in the US. Time and again, Trump plays on dark sentiments among his supporters about race and ethnicity - perhaps because he deeply believes it, perhaps for political gain. Either way, Trump has further normalized racism in his country. Words have consequences. In a country bulging with firearms, it is dangerous to use such dog whistles. Trump wrote in an enigmatic message on Twitter that he too is in favor of better background checks on firearm buyers, provided Congress approves stricter immigration laws. With this, Trump is letting himself in on it: he is not actually interested in a solution, but is turning it into a political game. "" I alone can fix it "", Trump said in 2016. Now he has the social mission of fulfilling that promise. It is time to come up with measures that the people have long supported. And he will have to face the consequences of his rhetoric.

De Croo: 'We repatriate six orphans of IS fighters' ""This is about six children who no longer have parents,"" Development Minister Alexander De Croo clarified Thursday on Radio 1. 'The choices their parents made are forgivable and we cannot condone them, but those are their parents' choices. Some of those children have also been abducted and are there (in the camps, ed.) in sometimes terrible conditions. According to De Croo, all the children were born in Belgium; two of the six are under the age of 10. 'For all the children, extensive analysis was done by military intelligence and eventually by OCAD, the Coordination Body for Threat Assessment. The OCAD says it is acceptable for each of those six children to be taken back. As a federal government and as a minister, you have to have confidence in those services. We cannot let them cremate. Each child will receive customized counseling in our country after repatriation. For now, it is assumed that these six children will remain. ""This is not an easy operation, which is why we also tried to group this together,"" De Croo said. According to him, there is ""absolutely no question"" that parents of Belgian children staying in the camps in Kurdish territory will be taken back in the future. The intention is for repatriation to follow as soon as possible. However, an agreement with Iraqi authorities is still needed. These live at odds with the Kurds, so another round of negotiations may be necessary. The mission does have some operational issues. The children must first be transferred from the camps to the city of Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan. From there, the Belgian military will repatriate them by military flight to Brussels. Belgium is following the example of other countries. Early this week, two more children from Syria were handed over to Dutch diplomats on the spot. The children aged 2 and 4 had a Dutch mother and a Belgian father from Maaseik in Limburg. Their father died some time ago on the battlefield, while their mother died recently due to the dire conditions in the camp. The children are the last legacy of Islamic State, which has been defeated in Iraq and Syria. The remnant fighters and sympathizers went underground; thousands died on the battlefield or in bombing raids. France only evacuated 12 children from northern Syria. Sweden, Norway and Germany have also repatriated a number of children in recent weeks. That all the countries are firing into action together is no accident. The Kurds have long been demanding that foreign governments remove their nationals from the refugee camps. The Kurds want to completely dismantle the camps as they are emptying and conditions there are worsening,"" Belgian government sources said. Therefore, children whose identity has been established are now being offered by the Kurds with an urgent request to take them back. Belgium long maintained its stance of not actively repatriating. It received buckets of criticism for that. A team of experts from the Free University of Brussels (VUB) led by psychologist Gerrit Loots is currently on site to assist the children. Loots and Co. urged the government to deliver travel documents so they could repatriate some children. But the government didn't want to know about that. Families of children in former IS territory also litigated against the Belgian state. Belgium initially obtained court orders to repatriate the children, under penalty of fines. But the government won on appeal, removing the legal pressure.

Column Michel Krielaars Infected youths beating up migrants 'I almost exploded with anger when my country took in only 12 refugees,' says Czech Marek Sindelka (b. 1984) on May 16 in Amsterdam, where he is participating in the European Night of Literature. ""When even our foreign minister added that we couldn't do more, I was so embarrassed that I had to respond. And I could only do that through literature."" It yielded the 2018 novel Material Fatigue, in which Sindelka denounces the Czech government's refugee policy without becoming moralistic. For example, he describes the human body as a material and conduit of experiences through two brothers who fled to Europe and lost each other along the way. One of them is smuggled into the Czech Republic under the hood of a car. Sindelka: ""In Material Fatigue, the body is primarily a burden, something that works against you because of its external characteristics, so you have to prove at every checkpoint that you are not a threat. While everyone forgets that we are all equal precisely by virtue of our bodies. Your body is the only thing you really own."" In the Czech Republic, anti-migration politics prevail during the upcoming European elections. It gives some Czechs a license to set up paramilitary vigilantes and rip off migrants. ""It is a striking number of young people who are guilty of this,"" said Sindelka. ""From bearers of humanistic values, they have degenerated into people infected with bullshit."" The Czech Republic is struggling with an explosion of far-right parties. One is led by Tomio Okamura, a Czech with a Korean-Japanese father, who is opposed to Gypsies in addition to migrants. ""Such a person, who is himself a kind of migrant, embodies the idiocy of the situation. For example, at one Prague station recently, Nicholas Winton - a German Jew who allowed hundreds of Jewish children to flee by train to England during the war - was commemorated, while at another station, migrants in transit to Germany were arrested and stamped on their hands."" Thirty years after the fall of the Wall, the Czech Republic no longer appears to be the country where a dissident writer like Vaclav Havel could become president. Sindelka: ""We have a very different kind of politics today, with a businessman as prime minister, who owns all the agriculture in our country like a mafia boss. A debate on human values is therefore impossible. Someone like Havel is hated, even though we have the lowest unemployment ever and salaries are rising."" Asked where this aggression comes from, Sindelka replied, ""Under communism, we were a closed society, not interacting with foreign cultures. As a result, the older generation in particular fears migrants. The terrorist attacks have reinforced that fear. While most migrants are not terrorists, even though President Zeman makes that connection to win voters."" Those hoping that the younger generation will provide change are wrong, Sindelka says. ""They experience freedom as a burden, as if paralyzed by all the opportunities to travel and study abroad. Except on Facebook, they don't seem to share their existence with anyone else, when that's what it's all about. They live as if in an endless childhood.""

Mahdi asks parties not to give false hope to hunger strikers: ""We are very worried about the condition"" State Secretary for Asylum and Migration Sammy Mahdi asks parties not to give false hope to hunger strikers. ""Giving a short stay to all hunger strikers is undesirable. A few months later, those same undocumented people are again in illegal residence. Moreover, the hunger strikers themselves have indicated that they do not want a temporary, but a permanent and collective residence permit for all sans papiers,"" he responded Monday night. Coalition partner PS called on the federal government earlier in the day to grant short-stay visas to the hunger strikers in order to create bargaining space with the undocumented people who went on hunger strike. Secretary of State Sammy Mahdi says he has been doing his utmost for weeks to convince people that a hunger strike makes no sense. The accusation of inaction is regrettable given the efforts that have been made for weeks, he believes. Over the past few days, Mahdi has been working with various partners to install a neutral zone, where hunger strikers can get clarity on existing procedures. This very week that neutral zone must and will be in place, the Mahdi administration said. Conversations. Sammy Mahdi has had several conversations with about a dozen organizations in recent weeks, as well as with the sans papiers themselves. ""My job is to engage with them and also clarify honestly what the policy stands for. Asylum seekers fleeing war are entitled to protection, students who follow the rules can study here, and people who want to come here to work can apply from abroad. And in exceptional humanitarian cases, we apply regularization for undocumented migrants precisely because we stand for a humane policy. We are very worried about the condition of the hunger strikers, but that should not force the policy in a certain direction,"" the secretary of state concluded. Despite many conversations, there often appears to be a great deal of ignorance about regularization. For example, it refers to Covid measures for people in illegal residence in countries such as Portugal, even though the temporary measures in those countries have already ended. Also in terms of access to the labor market, it seems more appropriate to ease the labor market for people who are here legally and, in addition, to fight against rogue employers who exploit people in illegal residence. ""The Inter-Ministerial Conference (IMC) can certainly serve to activate people who are here lawfully. On that front, things cannot progress fast enough. With unemployment rates as high as 39% in some regions, there is clearly still room for improvement.""

Italy Italian election winner seeks to reassure EU and financial markets 21:41 The radical-right populist Brothers of Italy won as much as 26 percent in Sunday's Italian parliamentary election. But there will be no big victory party or triumphant press conference. President Giorgia Meloni urged her fellow party members to be serious and sober. The situation in the country is serious, and a herculean task awaits the new, yet-to-be-formed government. A solution to the skyrocketing energy prices that are hitting Italian families and businesses hard is imminent. In doing so, the new administration must also draft the budget quickly. That new government is still some time away, by the way, as formation negotiations will not begin until after the new Italian parliament has had its inaugural session on Oct. 13. But with such a clear election result - the right-wing electoral alliance won a clear majority in parliament - it does seem obvious that President Sergio Mattarella will soon leave the initiative for government formation to Meloni. Second tranche of 21 billion euros. Europe and international markets are especially looking forward to whoever is appointed on Economy and Finance. Italy is the third largest economy in the euro zone, but it is also a debt-laden country, as well as the main beneficiary of the Next Generation EU European coronary fund, with more than 200 billion euros in the coming years. On Tuesday, the European Commission said that Italy will be given the green light for a second tranche of 21 billion euros after the requested targets are met. There are signs that the new administration is seeking continuity. The Italian economy desperately needs the European billions in the coming years. Meloni seems well aware of that. According to Italian media, she is considering a former top executive of the Italian National Bank for the important post of Finance. That is already a contrast to four years ago. After the last election, the radical-right Lega party in particular insisted that Paolo Savona, a euro-critical economist who described the euro as ""a German cage,"" become finance minister. Head of State Sergio Mattarella then held up Savona's appointment. There are signs that the new Italian government team is seeking continuity. Meloni's transition team is briefed on the country's financial and economic situation by Draghi's staff, and would also ask for some ideas for the budget. By Oct. 15, the European Commission expects a draft budget from Rome, which may yet be presented by the Draghi government. Then the new Italian government will have a chance to update that budget. It should all exude seriousness and responsibility, and certainly reassure international financial markets in addition to Europe. For now, that strategy is working. The international ratings agency S&P does not immediately foresee a risk in the transition to a new Italian government, it sounded just after the ballot. Confrontation Europe shuns. Meloni also seems to want to avoid confrontation with Europe for the time being in other key ministerial posts. Matteo Salvini of the Lega party may put away his dream of becoming Interior Minister again. Salvini closed Italy's borders to NGO boats, and his immigration policy put him on a collision course with the European Union. On Sunday, Salvini's Lega failed to reach 9 percent. Electorally, he weighs too lightly for such an important ministerial post. Finally, Silvio Berlusconi, the second coalition partner Meloni needs for her majority, also does not seem to have to count on a very visible role internationally. For that, especially outside Italy, he is too controversial. Meloni would, however, consider Berlusconi's party colleague Antonio Tajani, possibly as president of either chamber of parliament. Tajani likes to see himself at Foreign Affairs. The former president of the European Parliament is moderate and pro-European. This would immediately reassure Europe that Italy is not breaking European solidarity on sanctions against Moscow.

Is failing climate policy a human rights violation? 06:41 in Domestic , Foreign The European Court of Human Rights is considering several important climate cases. Are governments doing enough to combat climate change? Will a key element of the landmark Urgenda case apply to the entire European Union and even more countries? That question is on the table as the European Court of Human Rights considers today whether a country violates human rights if it does too little to combat climate change. If the answer is ""yes,"" legal experts say it will affect all of the nearly 50 countries affiliated with the human rights treaty. In the case brought by action group Urgenda against the Dutch state, the Supreme Court ruled in 2019 that the government is obliged to do more to combat ""dangerous climate change."" The Supreme Court stated that the European human rights treaty requires member states to protect their residents from ""real and immediate risks."" And, the Supreme Court concluded, there is global agreement on the extent to which climate change poses a threat. Three important climate cases are in play at the European Court, two of them today. One involves a group of Swiss elderly women, who argue that seniors' lives are at risk from increasing heat. The other was brought by a French former mayor, who believes the French government is not doing enough to combat warming and thus sea level rise, which could affect his municipality (near Dunkirk). A third case involves a group of Portuguese youths aged 12 to 21. They have sued dozens of countries, including the Netherlands, holding it responsible, in particular, for increasingly bad forest fires in their country. This case will be heard later this year. The youth believe that countries are negligent because their future is threatened by the disastrous effects of climate change. Dutch lawyers are following what is now happening at the European Court with great interest. Human rights also played an important role in the climate case against Shell, won by Milieudefensie two years ago. Lawyer in both the Urgenda and Shell climate cases is Dutch lawyer Roger Cox. He believes that if the European Court rules that countries must indeed do more for the climate, it will have a ""huge scope"" in Europe. That case confirms that failure to meet climate goals means human rights violations, including in the Netherlands. In addition, with such a ruling in hand, the Dutch government could urge other countries to do more. ""This is important,"" Cox said, ""because it will lead to faster international climate action."" The European Court of Human Rights gives great weight to these climate cases, says Urgenda lawyer Dennis van Berkel. He advised the Swiss women, and is at the Strasbourg court today. He said the importance is evidenced by the fact that the cases are heard by the ""Grand Chamber.""

Ukraine In Kiev, the EU shows its solidarity with Ukraine With a sizeable delegation, Von der Leyen wanted to convey that Ukraine is not alone. Yet expectations of a quick entry into the union were also tempered. The journey was the message. It was her fourth visit, EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Thursday, standing next to President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kiev. And this time she had not come alone. As many as 15 Eurocommissioners had traveled along for a meeting with the Ukrainian government. Another Zelensky summit with Von der Leyen and EU Council President Charles Michel will follow this Friday. With the two-day meeting just before the anniversary of Putin's invasion on Feb. 24, the EU wanted to underscore that Ukraine is not alone in the fight and will not go it alone. That message was addressed to both Ukraine and Russia. President Putin, meanwhile, took advantage Thursday of the 80th anniversary of the Soviet victory at Stalingrad to issue threats toward the West. ""We are threatened by German tanks again,"" he said, referring to the West's recent decision to give German-made Leopard 2 tanks to Ukraine. ""Those who think they will win on the battlefield evidently do not understand that a modern war with Russia will be fundamentally different for them. We do not send our tanks to their border. But we have a way to respond and that will not stop with the deployment of armored vehicles. Everyone should understand that,"" Putin said in what looked like a new disguised threat of nuclear weapons. The EU stands by beleaguered Ukraine with financial and economic support, funding arms supplies and hosting refugees. In total, the EU and member states have put 50 billion euros on the table, 37.8 billion in financial and humanitarian aid and 12 billion in military aid. In its luggage, the Commission had a few more news items on Thursday. It puts 25 million euros on the table for demining areas recaptured from Russia. It also doubles the number of Ukrainian military trained in the EU from 15,000 to 30,000 soldiers. Von der Leyen also announced that there will be an international center in The Hague to do preparatory work to try the Russian leadership for its part in the invasion of Ukraine. The center will coordinate the collection of evidence as well as prepare indictments. ""We will be able to start very soon,"" Von der Leyen said. ""Russia must be held accountable for its egregious crimes."" The EU has long been looking for ways to assist Ukraine in war crimes trials. For example, the Netherlands already sent forensic experts. Ukraine Tribunal. The International Criminal Court in The Hague is also already dealing with war crimes in Ukraine, but has no jurisdiction to judge the decision to invade. The new International Center for the Prosecution of Crime of Aggression should be the precursor to a special Ukraine tribunal where Russian leaders can indeed be tried. So the EU delegation's main concern was to press Ukraine to its chest. But the EU summit, EU diplomats said beforehand, also had the goal of dampening Ukraine's enthusiasm about joining the EU soon. Ukraine received EU candidate status last spring and, like all prospective members, must now meet European criteria in a wide range of areas. That process normally takes years, but Ukraine recently said it hopes to join in 2026. The European baggage therefore includes the message that Ukraine must meet the same requirements as everyone else. Progress is good and the EU hopes Kiev can keep up the momentum despite the burden of the war, but no one wants to commit to dates, a diplomat said. One issue on which Ukraine traditionally scored poorly was corruption.

Ecology Nature policy, built up over decades, is being scrapped As nature continues to deteriorate, the VVD wants to lower the bar for what nature is just a little. Hans Kampf feels ""grossly miffed."" Dutch nature policy, built up over decades, is in danger of creeping demolition. The idea of a Main Ecological Structure (EHS), a coherent network of existing and future natural areas, has existed since 1990, and has since served as an example for many countries in and outside Europe. Hans Kampf was senior policy advisor on Nature at the Ministry of Agriculture, Nature and Food Quality (LNV) and is a volunteer nature manager in a Natura 2000 low moor bog area near Utrecht. The Nature Policy Plan Nature for People, People for Nature (2000) solidified ""green"" and ""blue"" connections, with the financial basis for the sites of the Forestry Commission and those of private organizations such as Natuurmonumenten, provincial landscapes and a group of private landowners. The icing on the cake was Natura 2000, which, at the invitation of the European Commission, designated natural areas of special European significance. This in addition to the other natural areas as part of the EHS, which since 2013 has been called Natuurnetwerk Nederland. The Rutte I administration (2010-12) was a disaster for nature policy. Under State Secretary Henk Bleker (Agriculture and Nature, CDA), more than 100,000 hectares of connectivity zones and land acquisition were cut, while Staatsbosbeheer was slashed in the budget. Bleker and his political seconds acted as mouthpieces for the farmers who cause the agricultural nitrogen problem with their intensive methods, while farmers who advocate a different relationship with nature were not taken at face value. Balance of deterioration. It is obvious that this comes at the expense of livability, now and for future generations. The balance: peat meadows that continue to shrink due to continuous drainage for agricultural purposes; grasslands that still consist solely of a few high-yielding grasses without the flowering plants that are also important for our food because of pollinating insects. Explosions of pests due to the lack of ecological regulators; soils where soil life is eroding in quality even for sustainable agriculture due to permanent over-fertilization; biodiversity-less corn fields that can also take a lot of manure; meadow birds locked in reserves while farmers promised otherwise; a virtually treeless, high-speed demolished landscape for which farmers have supposedly guaranteed for decades. Nitrogen clouds everywhere, phosphate in the water of our natural areas, water that has gone from crystal clear to murky in a few years, resulting in a collapsed dragonfly population, butterflies under pressure. And so on. Nature gone, problem solved. But you can also say, as the VVD now seems to be doing with the trial balloon to ""adjust"" the protected status of some Natura 2000 areas, ""merge"" or eliminate smaller areas: nature gone, problem solved. Briefly then. As a retired senior policy advisor on Nature at the Ministry of Agriculture, Nature and Food Quality, I feel grossly miffed. Regarding the Natura 2000 and Habitat Directives, I count on Europe in any case. But for the preservation and restoration of our other natural areas - for ourselves, our children and future generations - it is all hands on deck regardless.

Opinion Jonas De Raeve Do we finally dare to look beyond the teaching certificate? 22 min Last week, the Flemish government selected for the first time 10 professions for which you can have competencies recognized and certified with a professional qualification. These competencies may be acquired through training or experience. A professional qualification should be worth as much in the labor market as an educational diploma. After all, they guarantee that the necessary competencies have been acquired, regardless of what training or experience preceded this. It is an important step toward competency-based thinking and much needed in a rapidly changing job market. But the potential of professional qualifications is much greater than we can estimate today. They could eventually shake up the entire education and training landscape and will allow workers to increase their employability. The government, education and training providers and also employers must then dare to take big steps forward. The coalition agreement already offers opportunities with the lifelong learning platform. The government could identify which competencies you already possess and which you still need to acquire to obtain a professional qualification. If, at the same time, it is clear via a learning account what training rights and budget you can use to follow additional training, we can really work on a learning culture in Flanders. Education will also have to embrace professional qualifications. Fearful of breaking their monopoly on degree delivery and on determining the content of educational curricula, they invariably put the brakes on policy discussions. However, vocational qualifications offer many opportunities to better match technical and labor market-oriented training to labor market needs in secondary education and to provide more flexible lifelong learning offerings in higher education. In addition, a vocational qualifying apprenticeship would be a good alternative for the group that cannot enter dual learning today because the school component is too heavy. Thus, we can finally reduce the unqualified outflow. Perhaps recognizing professional qualifications could even be part of the solution to the teacher shortage? If we make better use of the competencies available, perhaps we can still achieve the high ambition of raising the employment rate to 80%. Employers have created hundreds of professional qualifications in recent years. For nearly 500 occupations, they created a detailed list of required knowledge and skills needed to perform the job. Now it is time for this time investment to begin to pay off and for the qualifications to find their way into the job market. Employers can also do their part by recognizing the importance of professional qualifications in hiring and performance reviews. It helps them put the right employee in the right place, assess whether additional training or different job duties are feasible and what competencies still need to be acquired. A strong awareness campaign with concrete examples should support this. If we succeed in increasing the social value of vocational qualifications, we can make great strides in lifelong learning and eliminate the current mismatch between education and the labor market. If we make better use of the available competencies, perhaps we can still achieve the high ambition of the Flemish government to raise the employment rate to 80%. But then we will have to abandon the idea that only a teaching degree is blissful.

Consumer & Corona When will the bank defer my mortgage payments? This section addresses corona-related consumer law questions about work, finance and leisure. The issue. Even before Prime Minister Rutte coined the term ""intelligent lockdown,"" the first Dutch banks were at it: promising to help customers who ran into financial trouble as a result of the corona crisis. Making mortgage repayments was unnecessary for now, and interest payments were suspended, banks reported in mid-March. ""Banks are now part of the solution, not the problem,"" ABN Amro chief Kees van Dijkhuizen outlined the setup, citing the 2008 financial crisis. What exactly does this payment break look like? And to whom does it apply? Here's how it is. The answer to that question depends on the mortgage lender. Almost all have now rigged ""corona schemes"" for customers in financial trouble: from ABN Amro, ING and Rabobank to insurers like Aegon and new players like Munt Hypotheken and Florius. The idea behind it is the same: a payment break for customers in need. But because each financial institution has devised its own scheme, there is no set framework on the basis of which, as a homeowner, you can easily see whether you qualify for such a payment break and for how long. The payment break at ABN Amro, for example, applies by default for three months and (because of the rush due to the number of applications) may not take effect until June 1. ING, on the other hand, immediately suspends mortgage payments and uses ""a term by mutual agreement,"" instead of three months. Approaches to making up for missed mortgage payments also differ among mortgage lenders. At ABN Amro, the three missed months of interest and redemption are spread out over the period to Dec. 31, 2021, while Rabobank merely states, ""we'll make arrangements about that later."" The three largest banks do not charge additional fees for the missed months, they say. Mortgage payments must still be paid, but there is no additional cost to take advantage of the scheme. Thus, the ""late payment interest,"" which is normally charged when a mortgagee falls behind on repayment, does not apply. The contrast with Belgium, which also has a pay break, is considerable. The Belgian pause came about after consultations between the central bank, the finance ministry and the banking umbrella. As a result, a uniform maximum six-month payment break will apply to consumers who have no more than 25,000 euros in their savings accounts. ABN Amro, Rabobank and ING have no such financial buffer limit, they said when asked. ING stresses that customers should contact it and ""not wait until their buffer is completely gone."" ABN Amro says it is discussing with customers ""whether a payment break is the best solution."" ""If there is (a lot of) savings present, it is obvious that the customer will use it first."" Dutch banks' criteria ""are rather vague,"" notes attorney Thomas van Vugt of AMS Lawyers. Above all, the key question remains unclear: when are your financial problems serious enough to qualify for the break? Van Vugt points out that although the payment break is a gesture by the bank, this does not mean that the bank may use it arbitrarily. The banks decided to make the offer, and that brings with it certain responsibilities and a duty of care. ""If people substantiate that they have financial problems or foresee them as a result of the coronavirus, then as a bank you cannot simply say that someone is not entitled to the payment break. When in doubt, the decision should be in favor of the customer."" The answer. Because each mortgage lender has designed its own corona scheme, there is no uniform rule for who gets a payment break on their mortgage and for how long it applies. The pay break is a gesture and not a right. Nevertheless, mortgage lenders - now that they offer the breaks - may not simply refuse them if customers plausibly demonstrate that they have financial corona problems. Camil Driessen.

Need for European solidarity more than ever The global shock of the corona pandemic affects all European countries. Europe is experiencing its worst health crisis since the Spanish flu. European economies will suffer much more damage than initially thought. Therefore, a well-coordinated policy response is needed, both among member states and at the European level. It is crucial to minimize economic damage and maintain financial stability. Once the health crisis is under control, we must prepare for economic recovery. The seriousness of the medical situation and the extent of the expected economic and social damage makes European solidarity urgent. Member states have taken hefty fiscal measures against economic damage. Fiscal measures are estimated to average 2.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2020. Programs to support liquidity through government guarantees and tax deferrals for businesses and individuals exceed 13 percent of GDP. Complementing those national measures requires a coordinated approach at the European level. The European Commission has relaxed state aid rules and, together with the European Council, activated the ""escape clause"" of the budget rules, allowing countries to increase budget spending. Action by the European Central Bank is crucial to keep banks and financial markets functioning. The question is what else is possible now and in the near future at the European level. How can Europe quickly mobilize additional funding to support governments, businesses and citizens in all EU member states? In the short term and at least before 2020, European solidarity must be shaped by the rapid use of existing European institutions - the Commission, the Investment Bank (EIB) and the Stability Mechanism (ESM) - and the instruments at their disposal. The European Commission has announced unemployment insurance to secure as many jobs as possible. In addition, the 37 billion euros from the Corona Response Investment Initiative will be used to support health care, SMEs and the labor market. The European Investment Bank proposes a pan-European guarantee fund. In it, €25 billion worth of guarantees would come from member states, which could then be leveraged to mobilize an additional €200 billion for SMEs, midcaps and companies in the real economy. The European Emergency Fund ESM has 410 billion euros of ammunition and can provide credit at low interest rates. The ESM's toolbox includes different financial instruments for different circumstances. Currently, the so-called precautionary lines of credit - never before deployed - seem most appropriate. Such credits offer the advantage that money can flow quickly if a country needs urgent support because the facility is already in position. If the Investment Bank and the ESM push the gas pedal further, they will have to issue bonds to finance their lending. The Investment Bank - and to a lesser extent the Commission - issue such debt for all 27 member states, and the ESM emergency fund for the 19 eurozone countries. Those three institutions have been issuing so-called mutualized debt securities, i.e. European debt, for years. Today they have about 800 billion euros of debt outstanding. All three provide financing at interest rates well below the financing cost of most member states. They have also proven to be efficient and successful even in the face of substantial economic headwinds. This time they can do even more. Proposals are circulating to create new institutions or new financial instruments. But that takes time, time we don't have. At the beginning of the euro crisis, the first temporary bailout fund, the European Financial Stability Facility, took seven months to issue its first bond. And that was already one with a rocky pace compared to similar institutions, which took three years. Creating new European debt requires capital, guarantees or allocated revenues, as well as a well-functioning legal and governance system. Therefore, it is best to use all the existing institutions and instruments that have been successfully mobilizing large sums for years. Looking beyond 2020, solutions beyond that are possible and necessary to help European economies recover from this shock. As announced by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the next multi-year budget focuses on combating the economic impact of the corona crisis. The focus could then be on member states facing particularly negative economic consequences. For the next few years, Italy best not be a net contributor to the European budget. In addition, the EIB may increase its capital to lend more money in the coming years. And the ESM has borrowing capacity available.

New CEO Mercedes struggles with legacy from past 'We would have loved to welcome you to our booth in Geneva, but health is more important.' As the world's most important auto show was canceled due to the encroaching corona virus, Daimler CEO Ola Källenius addressed the press in a teleconference on Tuesday. Although more and more carmakers are staying away from expensive saloons, the successor to legendary Mercedes executive Dieter Zetsche swears allegiance to the concept. 'Car shows remain attractive; we'll come back as soon as we can.' Källenius (50) has his hands full with the coronavirus. Daimler's factories in China, which closed a week longer early this year, are getting back up to cruising speed. In the European plants, the virus is not causing any problems for the time being, according to the CEO. 'Our supply chain is global. We work closely with our suppliers in China. It is too early to say what the total impact will be. Our team looks in detail at what happens in every factory in the world. It's day-to-day management. Like the competition, Källenius expects a temporary slump in car sales. ""Corona certainly put a damper on sales in China in the first quarter. But I remain cautiously optimistic about the underlying demand for cars. Thanks to the refreshed model lineup, Mercedes posted record sales in 2019. But that growth did not translate into profits. Daimler's auto branch saw its ebitda halve to 3.4 billion euros last year. Källenius attributes that decline mainly to ""issues from the past. While rival Volkswagen was labeled a diesel sundowner with its tampering software, Daimler did not prove to be the good guy either. The German government fined the company 870 million euros last year for manipulated emissions values. The question of whether he expects any more problems causes Källenius to stutter. 'Some proceedings are still ongoing.... Euh, it's not wise to talk about details when we're still talking to governments. Daimler is also chasing in the electric field. Only last year did it launch its first all-electric model, the large SUV EQC. Daimler is mainly counting on Smart for electrification. Mercedes is now positioning the city car, which never really made a profit, as an all-electric brand. Before that, Källenius parked Smart in a joint venture with Chinese group Geely. Li Shufu, the owner of Geely, recently became a major shareholder in Daimler and he owns Volvo. About synergies with the Swedish premium brand, Daimler's Swedish CEO remains on the record. 'Our cooperation with Geely is going very well,' says Källenius. 'Thanks to Geely, we are increasing our footprint. That could lead to greater opportunities. I can't say anything concrete about that today, but we are open to the possibilities. Daimler urgently needs to sell more electric cars if it does not want to pay European millions in fines. Tighter CO2 emissions targets are a problem for the heavy Mercedes fleet. '2020 and 2021 will be a challenge. We are within shooting distance, although everything depends on sales. But mentally and technically we made the click. We want our cars to be carbon neutral by 2039 at the latest.' Unlike other automakers, Mercedes refuses to write off the classic internal combustion engine. 'The internal combustion engine will be with us for a long time. By 2030, 50 percent of our sales must be electric or hybrid. So it will still exist after 2030. I don't want to put a date on the internal combustion engine. It's still important to make those more efficient. The malaise at Mercedes is making itself felt on the stock market. A Daimler share, worth 93 euros five years ago, costs 38 euros today. ""There is a general nervousness in the market about the transformation of the auto industry,"" Källenius says. 'That applies to almost all car companies. Where will the journey to electrification end? What is the impact of digitization? How do we transform our business model? Those questions will play out for several more years.

Politicians do listen to proposal from French-speaking scientists, but barbers immediately shoot down plan: ""Where do you draw the line?"" The scientists - epidemiologist Marius Gilbert (ULB) and infectiologists Nathan Clumeck (CHU Sint-Pieter) and Leila Belkhir (UZ Sint-Lucas, Woluwe) - propose in an opinion piece in the newspaper ""Le Soir"" that a ""Covid safe"" label should henceforth be awarded to establishments based on a number of parameters, such as good ventilation, duration of exposure or mouth masking. They additionally advocate divisions within sectors, and want self-testing to play a role as well. That way, they want to avoid yo-yo movements, where sectors have to keep closing and reopening. ""We took this initiative based on what all is happening now,"" Professor Clumeck explained Monday night on ""Terzake. According to the infectiologist, for many people, the strain is out after a year of corona measures. ""There are gatherings of young people, illegal restaurants and most recently (in Antwerp, ed.) the tragedy of the boy who died trying to flee from the police."" According to Clumeck, we are therefore at a breaking point in Belgium. ""If we do nothing and continue like this, I fear there will be more protests, resulting in more repression and possibly more violence."" Political interest. The proposals already have the support of the French-speaking federal majority parties. For PS Chairman Paul Magnette, it is ""a very interesting contribution to the debate on the evolution of our strategy. In addition to vaccination, a serious course of action is to phase out of the current carcan. I want the proposal to be thoroughly examined as soon as possible,"" the president of the French-speaking Socialists announced on Twitter. Flemish mayors are also showing interest. At the local level, Flemish mayors also seem to have ears for the proposal. ""This certainly offers opportunities to gradually come back out of the lockdown, because people are getting tired of it,"" Wim Dries (CD&V), mayor of Genk and president of the Association of Flemish Cities and Municipalities, told VRT NWS. And Aalsters Mayor Christoph D'Haese (N-VA) also called the ideas of the French-speaking scientists ""a constructive approach because we really do have to start looking at this health crisis in a different way."" According to D'Haese, there is too much focus on corona numbers and not enough on mental well-being and the economy. ""Where do you draw the line?"" However, among the Belgian Beauty Federation and United Hairdressers, two federations for hairdressers and beauticians in our country, the enthusiasm is a lot less than among politicians. Many hairdressers and beauticians do not see a division in terms of treatments, according to the federations. ""Where do you ultimately draw the line? Then a barber is not going to be able to open the door, and the vast majority of beauty salon treatments are done in the face, so they will remain closed as well."" According to the federations, there is no significant difference between contact occupations in terms of infection rate, ""so the theory is wrong."" The proposal to add self-testing to the current protocol also falls on a cold stone. The federations cite a survey that would show that six in 10 (surveyed) salon owners no longer want an additional measure. ""There is no sector that has had so many measures imposed on it and that with the promise that we could stay open,"" said Mario Blokken, president of the Belgian Beauty Federation. ""While medical contact professions such as dentists and physiotherapists do not even have to apply half as many measures. Continuing this unreasonable approach is unmentionable for the industry. We no longer accept two weights and measures for the contact professions."" The federations maintain that they nevertheless remain ""constructive."" Further, it sounds that the barbers and beauty specialists are simply counting on being able to reopen on April 26, the date that was predetermined that they would have to remain closed at least until then. The federations also argue that a financial recovery plan is ""a must.""

Doing Green With tens of thousands not buying clothes for a summer Every week NRC guides you toward sustainable living. You have six more days to make your move in the sale before the 2019 Slow Fashion Season begins on June 21. It would actually be better called No Fashion Season, because it is a global action in which people promise not to buy clothes for three calendar months. That is, no new ones. Exchanges and buying second-hand are allowed. This is the second time the action has been organized. Last year, 2,625 people participated. At the time of writing, nearly 5,500 people have committed through slowfashionseason.org . The goal is 10,000 non-buyers; registration is open until next Friday. That we all buy way too many clothes should come as no surprise; just look at the barely-worn or even completely unworn pieces that you yourself undoubtedly have in your closet. Collaction, the organization behind the action, cites a few figures on the environmental impact of the fashion industry. Each year, 32 million Olympic-sized swimming pools of water are used - just making a cotton T-shirt requires 2,700 liters - and the industry accounts for 8 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. Then there's dyeing (""the biggest polluter of clean water after agriculture""), the huge amount of clothes thrown away and the, to put it mildly, not ideal working conditions under which many clothes are produced, among other things. If 10,000 people do not buy new items for three months, 360 million liters of water will be saved and 1.4 million fewer kilograms of CO 2 will be emitted, according to Collaction. Malpractice. Aren't you depriving textile workers who already have so little of much needed work with the action? Slow Fashion Season's Dutch ambassador, Babette Porcelijn, doesn't think so. Porcelijn is the author of the book The Hidden Impact (2017), in which she exposes the environmental impact of our consumption behavior. Clothing ranks number eight on her top ten polluting consumption list, right after the bathroom category, assuming that the average Dutch person buys three items of clothing, each weighing half a kilo a month. ""There are so many abuses in the garment industry that I see it as a modern form of slavery. The system is just not right. If you want to offer something to the people there, you better look for fair trade clothing."" For Porcelain himself, by the way, the action is hardly a sacrifice. ""I already buy very little.""

Top Kim-Putin Kim warns: only peace if US adopts more lenient stance The North Korean leader is not satisfied with the outcome of his latest meeting with Trump, he revealed during his visit to Russia. Only if the United States becomes more flexible and weakens sanctions against North Korea can the impasse in negotiations be broken. That is what North Korean leader Kim Jong-un told Russian President Vladimir Putin during the summit in Vladivostok, North Korean state news agency KCNA reported. According to Kim, tensions with the US could easily return. He says he is prepared for ""every possible outcome."" The North Korean leader also told Putin that the US was ""in bad faith"" at the denuclearization summit between Trump and Kim in the Vietnamese capital Hanoi. Kim had also previously expressed his unhappiness with the outcome of that February summit, which ended prematurely. He even threatened to resume testing nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles if sanctions against his country are not lifted. He did say earlier this month that he was still open to a third summit with Trump. Solid discussion. Kim and Putin met for the first time on Thursday. In front of the press, the two shook hands in Vladivostok, in Russia's far east. They then held talks with each other behind closed doors. It was the first time in eight years that the heads of state of Russia and North Korea have met. At the time, Kim's father Kim Jong-il met with then-Russian President Dimitri Medvedev. Putin said after the summit that the two had had ""a solid discussion."" The leaders discussed, among other things, how to resolve the conflict on the Korean Peninsula. In addition, Putin promised to help end the ""nuclear standoff"" and said his country wants to help Kim ""normalize ties between North Korea and the United States."" However, he did not mention any concrete solutions or measures. Kim called it ""a fruitful conversation"" afterwards, and at the end of the summit, the North Korean leader invited Putin to Pyongyang. The Russian president responded, according to KCNA. The White House has not yet responded to Kim and Putin's statements. A U.S. diplomat did say that North Korea's attempts to connect with Russia prove that sanctions against the North Korean regime are working.

comment Dredger could have known what it was doing in Angola Is it acceptable to win large, lucrative contracts in countries that don't take human rights very seriously? And at what price? Is it acceptable to win large, lucrative contracts in countries that do not take human rights seriously? And at what price? That Dutch companies may pay bribes for foreign contracts is well known - virtuous does not. Consider the investigations into unfair trade practices by shipbuilder Damen, offshore company SBM, development bank FMO. When human rights are violated, moral responsibility weighs more heavily. Last weekend, more was revealed about the roles of dredging company Van Oord, ING and the Dutch state's credit insurer Atradius in a major urban renewal project, Corimba Boulevard, in the Angolan capital, Luanda. To make that possible, three thousand families were forcibly evicted from their homes. Some of them now live in a garbage dump. ""Army and police arranged to deprive residents of food and hardly any water for a week, beating residents and spraying with tear gas and hot water cannons,"" wrote Trouw, which interviewed evicted residents. The publication came as part of the ICIJ, the international consortium of investigative journalists, on the Angola land grab. And the billions that disappeared in the process into the pockets of Isabel dos Santos, the daughter of the former president. ICIJ obtained 715,000 documents from Dos Santos' private administration through African whistleblowers. The estimated wealth of this ""richest woman in Africa"" is two billion euros. A Dos Santos company, Urbinvest, was client of the ""Corimba Boulevard"" for which Van Oord would connect several islets off the coast of the metropolis of millions. ING helped finance the project by providing a $400 million (over 360 million euros) loan to the Angolan state. Atradius insured that sum. The Dutch companies now say they did not know about the forced moves nor about Dos Santos' reputation. That defense is weak: Dos Santos has been under fire since 2013 for the dubious origin of its billions. For this project, her company claimed millions in vague costs. Experts say in both papers that several ""red flags"" for possible corruption have been blatantly ignored. Van Oord could have known about the evictions. The company says it only signed the contract in 2016, but the documents show that talks about the project were underway before the three thousand families were evicted. That Minister Sigrid Kaag (Foreign Trade, D66) now wants to talk to Van Oord is a first step. But a slap on the wrist by the Cabinet gives no guarantee that Dutch companies will then show social responsibility. For that, the rules are simply too lenient - and the loopholes too wide. Perhaps the settlements that the prosecution tends to make in such cases are not so apt to raise moral standards after all. The fact that shadowy constructions run through the Netherlands, as the investigation shows, doesn't help either. Many of Dos Santos' interests in oil telecom and diamond companies were handled through Dutch letterbox firms. The Dutch Central Bank had these tax shortcuts in its sights as early as 2012. But again, signaling is not yet punishing. Better supervision is needed, as is more self-understanding and clearer moral frameworks. Enforcement is always a capstone. Deal on historic cut in oil production is in place After days of negotiations, the ball seems to be in the court. During final consultations Sunday night, the member states of the Opec oil cartel reached an agreement with a host of other oil producers such as Russia, Mexico and the United States to cut oil production. This was confirmed by Saudi, Kuwaiti and Mexican ministers. As of May 1, Opec+ - an alliance of Opec members that includes producers such as Russia, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Oman and Sudan - was pumping 9.7 million barrels less oil daily. That amounts to some 10 percent of global production. The measure will remain in effect for at least two months. Never before did oil producers agree on such a large production cut. The historic deal was largely in place by Friday. Saudi Arabia and Russia would each cut 2.5 million barrels while the remaining Opec+ member states would together pump another 5 million barrels less each day. But they coupled this with an important condition. The United States and Mexico should also make an effort. Otherwise, the demarche may well be a slap in the face and the desired effect - a rise in the price of oil - may fail to materialize. Mexico, however, played the game hard. It did not see fit to cut its production by 400,000 barrels a day. That persistence seems to have paid off. Under Sunday night's deal, the contents of which have not yet been officially disclosed, the Latin American country should eventually drop its production by only 100,000 barrels per day. According to news agency Bloomberg, theUnited States, Canada and Brazil together are scaling back their daily production by 3.7 million barrels. That they agreed to that measure is not too big a surprise. Due to the corona pandemic and its associated impact on the economy, demand for the black gold was down anyway. Analysts estimate that demand is down by a third now that about half the world's population is in a lockdown regime. The key question is whether the historic deal is enough to put a floor under oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent oil fell to its lowest level in 18 years due to the corona crisis. Recently, it even dipped below $25 a barrel for a while. Goldman Sachs and UBS predicted last week that a 15 percent contraction in oil production would not even be enough to stop the price drop. They did not rule out a drop in the price of a barrel of Brent oil to $20, down from $70 at the beginning of the year.

NU+ | Will energy companies benefit from price cap? 'Books must open' The surprise was palpable when the ACM came to the House of Representatives last week to explain its oversight of energy companies' profits. The watchdog must ensure that companies maintain no more than a ""reasonable"" profit margin, but could not say what then is reasonable. That is secret. If it becomes known how much profit is considered reasonable, all companies would start making that maximum profit, according to the ACM. So then prices go up even further. Therefore, even the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate does not know how much profit the regulator considers reasonable. ""Wow,"" responded SP MP Renske Leijten. She fears that it will become uncontrollable whether the billions of dollars in energy subsidies are going to the right places. ""The ACM is asking us to trust them on their blue eyes. I don't,"" she tells NU.nl. Court is critical. Oversight of the regulator is now there only when energy companies go to court. Earlier this year, the Trade and Industry Appeals Tribunal ruled on another case between the ACM and Essent. According to the regulator, Essent had overcharged for power in 2018. But the court strongly criticized the ACM's secret model. The regulator may only use that model to signal when companies may be overcharging. The ACM cannot force a reduction in rates with only ""a reference to a (secret) assessment model."" Fear of high prices. Yet that model is now the government's main weapon to prevent excess profits at energy companies. On Tuesday, the House of Representatives passed several motions calling on the cabinet to keep tighter tabs on suppliers. It is not yet clear whether and how supervision of energy companies will be strengthened if the price cap is implemented. From left to right, political parties fear that suppliers could use the price cap to actually increase profits. Consumers will suffer much less next year when power and gas prices are high: the government will pay anything above the ceiling price anyway. Only when usage exceeds 1,200 cubic feet of gas and 2,900 kilowatt-hours of electricity do consumers start feeling the full energy price themselves. The government will have to look closely at the books of energy companies to prevent taxpayer money from going the wrong way, says energy economist Machiel Mulder of the University of Groningen. ""We no longer have any competition. Consumers have a guaranteed price and suppliers are reimbursed for their additional costs."" ""There is a risk that we are transferring many billions of too much tax money,"" thinks independent MP Pieter Omtzigt. ""The energy companies need to open all the books."" This is how the price cap works From January 1, maximum rates for energy will apply: 1.45 euros per cubic meter of gas (up to 1,200 cubic meters) and 40 euro cents per kilowatt hour (up to 2,900 kWh). The government transfers money to energy companies in advance. They must use that money to reimburse the difference between the market price and the ceiling price. Only afterwards is it checked whether all the money transferred has indeed reached the consumer, and whether the supplier is charging reasonable rates. The total cost of the price cap is highly uncertain, due to the highly volatile market prices for gas and electricity. The cabinet expects costs of between 10 and 40 billion euros over 2023. Expensive procurement. The price cap also removes the incentive for energy companies to buy competitively themselves. ""A company that doesn't procure properly will simply be reimbursed,"" Mulder said. The government then pays for the poor procurement strategy. Under the price cap, it will be difficult to judge companies on this, the professor believes. According to VVD MP Silvio Erkens, the cabinet should try that anyway. He wants the ministry to determine what purchasing prices are approximately reasonable. If companies have overpaid, they should pay for it themselves. ""You still have to keep an incentive so they buy in efficiently."" A spokesman for Energy Minister Rob Jetten said that work is still in progress to further develop the price cap. In doing so, the ministry is also looking at how oversight of billion-dollar payments to energy companies will work. More should become known in the coming weeks.

Shaky European unanimity: Bulgaria wants to renegotiate with Russians over gas Balkan Bulgaria has made a 180-degree turn toward Russia. The government supported Ukraine and subsequent European sanctions and was subsequently cut off from Russian gas. Meanwhile, an interim government is in power that cares little for European solidarity. The government is even seeking rapprochement with the Russians again, it was announced in a television interview this week. ""Talks are being held at the highest level,"" Prime Minister Galab Donev said. That announcement - that negotiations with Russia are underway - is causing great anxiety in capital Sofia. Hundreds of activists blocked the main entrance of the government building in recent days. They are demanding the resignation of the interim government that has been in power for less than a month. In front of the gate of the presidential palace, civic weight BOEC used a spray can to paint an accusatory ""Z,"" the symbol of support for Russia. A message to President Rumen Radev who appointed the new government. Leader of BOEC, Georgi Georgiev is clear: ""We demand the guarantee that Bulgaria will not reopen negotiations with Gazprom and believe that Bulgarian society has the strength to win this battle."" In capital Sofia, gas is used for communal district heating. Winters are considerably cold and in working-class neighborhoods, residents are already having high bills. At the district heating office, Bulgarians walk in and out with concerns about their payment. They have no problem with their country renegotiating with Gazprom. Pro-European Prime Minister Kiril Petkov came to power in December. He promised to end corruption and wanted independence from Russia. His government condemned Russian aggression in Ukraine and supported European sanctions. In late April, Gazprom turned off the tap to Bulgaria and Poland because of their refusal to pay in rubles. The two countries thus became the first European member states to be cut off from Russian gas. A difficult situation for Bulgaria, the country was 90 percent dependent on gas from Russia. Prime Minister Petkov then signed an agreement with the United States for the delivery of seven liquefied natural gas (lng) tankers to ""improve Bulgaria's energy security."" An agreement in which the European Commission mediated. But the Petkov government was overthrown after a vote of no confidence. President Radev appointed an interim government with an energy minister who quickly announced that ""it is practically inevitable that Bulgaria will negotiate with Gazprom Export for the recovery of gas resources under the current contract."" Bulgaria is one of the poorest member states of the European Union. Communist rule ended in 1989. Yet pro-Russian forces are still active in the Balkan country, a 2020 European think tank - the Center for the Study of Democracy - said. ""This U-turn is a dangerous development,"" analyzes Bulgarian Energy expert Kostantsa Rangelova. ""If Gazprom agrees to supply our gas again, it comes with significant obligations. What should we promise Gazprom that the gas will flow again? Into what trap will we fall in the coming years?"" Bulgaria is in a serious energy crisis. The country is said to have only 54 percent of its required gas supply in order, far below the European average . The seven US tankers would deliver about 1 billion cubic meters of lng from October this year to April 2023. The interim cabinet was to confirm the agreement with the U.S. supplier in mid-August, but ultimately chose to accept only one tanker. The outgoing Prime Minister Petkov also earlier initiated the construction of an interconnector gas pipeline between Greece and Bulgaria for gas from Azerbaijan.
