Energy crisis Emergency aid should bring South Africa out of the dark The South African government is intervening to ease the debts of energy company Eskom. Does that solve the years-long power crisis? South African government takes over half of energy company Eskom's debts. It involves a loan of more than 13 billion euros. With the aid, the state-owned company must pay off debts and interest obligations and pay for maintenance of coal-fired power plants. South Africa has been plagued by continuous power outages for 16 years due to mismanagement, corruption, theft and technical defects at the power plants. President Cyril Ramaphosa declared a state of emergency earlier this month because of power shortages, which reached a record last year. Some parts of the country are without power for up to six hours a day. Hospitals are unable to treat patients, businesses have to close and internationally, Africa's most industrialized country suffers great reputational damage. ""Our economy is at enormous risk,"" Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana said in his budget speech this week. ""Uncertainty is increasing, which requires us to do bold things."" If Eskom does not meet the conditions for debt relief, heads will have to roll, he later added during an interview with Reuters. That same evening, Eskom announced that director Andre de Ruyter was stepping down effective immediately. De Ruyter had already resigned in December but would stay on until March 31 so the company could find a replacement. Possibly he has now resigned anyway because Energy Minister Gwede Mantashe accuses him of being unable to solve the crisis. He would also have completely lost the support of President Ramaphosa. Band-Aids. South Africa has wanted to reorganize the state-owned utility for years because of a constant shortage of power for its population of 60 million. But it seems to be band-aiding a system that actually needs structural reorganization. The government's loan to Eskom comes with strict conditions. For example, the money may not be used for investments in green energy. This is notable because South Africa says it wants to stop coal production by 2030. The US, UK and European Union promised South Africa $8.5 billion for the transition to renewable energy. But the crisis seems to have put the energy transition on the back burner. Critics say the government appears to be looking for a quick fix ahead of the elections. ""The risk of that is that the next crisis will be even worse,"" says sociologist Bram Büscher of Wageningen University. The professor is also affiliated with the South African universities of Johannesburg and Stellenbosch. ""The other problems, like the dirty coal mines, are not going away with this loan.""

The U.S. Department of Justice will investigate the relationship between aviation manufacturer Boeing and authority Federal Aviation Administration. Prosecutors are fluffing out whether Boeing has exerted undue influence over the U.S. Aviation Authority in recent years, AP news agency reports. The Seattle Times goes even further in an analysis. Driven by budget cuts and a lack of time, aviation authority FAA is said to have given the aircraft manufacturer more and more responsibility itself. Specifically when it comes to the inspection of the Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft type, two of which crashed in the past six months. Hurry. It begins in 2015. Boeing is then trying to keep up with competitor Airbus and wants to get the latest aircraft, the 737 Max 8, to market as soon as possible. But the manufacturer is nine months behind its European competitor. Managers of aviation authority FAA are therefore exerting increasing influence over their safety inspectors; safety checks must be quick and the result must actually be preferably in Boeing's favor. If checks do take too long, or if safety inspectors say that some work needs to be done on the aircraft, FAA managers either rush approval through or delegate the safety checks to Boeing itself. ""There was no proper and complete review of the documents provided by Boeing. Reviews, above all, had to meet deadlines,"" one of the inspectors told The Seattle Times. In that hasty setting, the Boeing 737 Max 8's under-fire operating system was approved in no time, inspectors interviewed said. That very operating system, called MCAS, now seems to be exhibiting glitches that may have led to the two accidents in Ethiopia and Indonesia. The exact cause of the accidents, by the way, is not yet known. French aviation inspectors did announce last Monday that there were ""clear similarities"" between the crash of Ethiopian Airlines' Boeing 737 Max and that of Indonesia's Lion Air last October. The US aviation authority FAA also said last week it saw similarities between the two accidents involving the 737 Max 8 aircraft. Until then, the organization maintained that the Boeing aircraft was safe. FAA, unlike forty other countries around the world, did not find it necessary to ground the aircraft type. Until last Wednesday, that is. The two accidents involving the 737 Max 8 killed a total of 346 people. Also read: Boeing is no longer a success story. Aircraft maker Boeing was until recently considered primarily a success story . The 747 was called the ""Queen of the Sky,"" the 737 a blockbuster and a gold mine. Yet with the Tenerife collision, the company also has decades of the largest plane crash ever recorded.

Reportage Nursing Homes Residents with dementia stare out next to a teddy bear: 'It's painful' For bear hunting, you're in the right place on Lindenburgh Avenue, centrally located in the village. Behind many of Hof van Nassau's windows is a plush toy, illustrative of this corona time. Nice for passing children, but also for the needy elderly who often sit behind the same window. If a child notices the bear, the resident can immediately wave. Every moment of contact with the outside world is one, in this time of isolation. ""It's painful,"" sighed site manager Marcha Kwisthout. Especially here at Hof van Nassau, where the often demented residents are encouraged to leave their living rooms every day. People are supposed to be outside. At the complex there is a brasserie, there is a store, a hairdresser, a physical therapist. Wherever you go, there is never a way in. But many haven't touched their coats in ages. They sit at the communal table of the living group or in their own apartment. Staring outward next to a teddy bear, for example. The candle out. A year and a half is about the average length of stay here. Then the candle is out with vulnerable residents. It raises the question of taking so much away from people in that short period of time. They are not allowed outside and visitors are out of the question. It's an ethical dilemma of sorts, Kwisthout acknowledges. ""I see what effect the measures have, both emotionally and cognitively. Dementia is a progressive disease, thanks to our Active Aging program we can still positively influence the course. Now, of necessity, that is at a standstill. In addition, there is a great need for contact between residents and family members. But I also see the other side, how sick people can get from the virus. What weighs more heavily? Out of those evils, I cannot choose. I just assume that it is good to follow the advice of the professionals."" When the nursing homes had already been cut off from the outside world because of cabinet measures, at least here internal freedom remained intact for a while. Until the first contamination occurred and Court of Nassau had to tighten the rules. Kwisthout: ""We work with freedoms on four levels. I estimate that eighty percent of our residents have Freedom Grade 3. They are not allowed to go into the village by themselves, but they are allowed to go all over our complex. We had to revoke that freedom as well."" Fourteen residents have now contracted the virus. Some are emphatically on the mend, some have a considerable recovery time ahead of them. One woman died. Because Hof van Nassau consists of 15 residential groups of eight residents and most of the homes have not been affected, the virus is closer for some than others. Chatting spontaneously. The groups not in isolation can still go to the indoor garden with caregivers, according to Kwisthout. ""Only under supervision, then. But even then, the restriction of freedom does a lot. We have a resident who normally, because of her dementia, goes to the store as many as 10 times a day. She is now confronted ten times a day that it is not allowed. That gives a lot of grief."" As lively as it should be on nice days in Hof van Nassau, life there now stands still emphatically. If you walk around the back - the little harbor of Steenbergen on one side, the nursing home on the other - you walk past the empty terrace of the brasserie. If the stories are to be believed, it should always be crowded in the spring. Just as residents also regularly stop in at Kwisthout for a spontaneous chat. That takes time, far too much sometimes, but the site manager longs for it again. After all, it's a hundred times better than a resident waving at passing children all day.

Coronavirus/Covid-19 European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen: ""Without vaccine, avoid contact with elderly until end of this year"" Update Sun Apr 12 16:16 ""Without a vaccine, we should avoid contact with the elderly until the end of this year, especially if they live in rest homes."" So says President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen in an interview with the German newspaper Bild. Virologist Marc Van Ranst is more cautious. ""We won't be able to interact between generations in a normal way, but not seeing grandparents for so long seems difficult in practice."" When will corona measures relax? And how will that affect the pandemic? When will we be able to visit our family and friends again without worry? These are questions we have often asked ourselves in recent weeks. Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, does not shy away from giving a partial answer. In an interview with Bild, von der Leyen says contact with the elderly should be avoided until at least the end of this year. Especially the elderly who reside in residential care facilities, because they are especially vulnerable. ""That is difficult and the isolation weighs heavily, but it is a matter of life and death. We have to be patient and disciplined,"" von der Leyen said. But not everyone will have to remain in isolation for so long, according to the Commission President. Unlike seniors and people with a medical history, children and younger people will have more freedom to get around again sooner, von der Leyen believes. Virologist Marc Van Ranst doesn't want to go that far. ""It is clear that we will not deal in a normal way between different generations until there is a vaccine,"" he told VRT NWS. ""Only the timing of that vaccine is not set in stone, nor is its success as guaranteed as many believe. So we also need to look at other exit strategies."" ""It does seem hard not seeing grandparents for so long. That seems very difficult to put into practice,"" Van Ranst said. ""Bringing sick children to grandparents, we may never do it again. But if we all do our best now to comply with the measures, we can go for an exit strategy, which will make more possible than we have now. Perhaps visiting grandparents with a mouth mask would be an option."" European Union guidelines and recommendations for relaxing quarantine measures in member states are also coming in the coming weeks. A general date for such an easing is not something von der Leyen wants to impose, because the situation is different in all EU countries: ""I do not want to make general decisions, while the situation in Milan is completely different from that in Münster, and that there are great differences between urban and rural areas.""

For those who must close their doors, however, there will be appropriate support measures. The booster shot vaccination campaign should be accelerated , argues the Consultative Committee. ""Vaccines are still an extremely powerful weapon. For those who must close, there will be appropriate support measures , De Croo said. The next Consultation Committee will take place on December 15 , at which time the measures will be evaluated.

Coronacrisis Corona vaccines less effective in some patients undergoing cancer treatment Coronacrisis Corona vaccines less effective in some patients undergoing cancer treatment Patients make fewer antibodies, especially after their second shot. This is according to research conducted by the University Hospital of Antwerp (UZA). 10:19 Some cancer treatments reduce the efficacy of the Pfizer vaccine. Patients make fewer antibodies, especially after their second shot. This is according to research conducted by the University Hospital of Antwerp (UZA). Side effects in patients undergoing cancer treatment were also examined. Some patients undergoing cancer treatment produce fewer antibodies when vaccinated. This is according to a study by the University Hospital Antwerp, in collaboration with Sciensano and Fight Against Cancer. 200 cancer patients were administered the BioNTech/Pfizer vaccine for the study. Blood samples were taken at various times to examine the production of antibodies. Side effects were also thoroughly identified. The side effects were not too bad. These are ""comparable to reports made by healthy individuals,"" according to department head of oncology Marc Peeters (UZA), he says in the video below. Thus, patients undergoing cancer treatment have no more (or less) side effects than people without cancer. The Pfizer vaccine is as safe for cancer patients as it is for healthy volunteers. The immune system begins producing antibodies and neutralizing antibodies after the first shot. These are capable of eliminating the virus. This is true in healthy people and also in patients undergoing cancer treatment. However, antibody production after the first shot does not increase to the same extent in all groups of patients. After the second prick, Marc Peeters says there is a clear difference between healthy people and some groups of patients undergoing cancer treatment. ""Antibodies are produced in most patients, but to a lesser extent in some treatment groups."" Patients may be less protected against the coronavirus due to this reduced production of antibodies. Their immune response, according to the study, is ""delayed and less powerful, which can lead to breakthrough infections."" However, the reduced immune response is not there with all cancer treatments. In particular, patients receiving chemotherapy treatment produce fewer antibodies and neutralizing antibodies. ""Also, patients who were treated with the drug rituximab have a less potent immune response,"" said Marc Peeters. ""They made almost no antibodies."" Rituximab is used to treat lymphoma, among other things. It suppresses part of the immune system. Other cancer treatments seem to affect the effect of vaccination less. Thus, the immune response was quite normal in patients treated with immunotherapy and with hormonal treatments. Patients treated with chemotherapy make fewer antibodies after their second shot. fstop123. The study has practical implications. ""Cancer patients who produce fewer antibodies after their second vaccination are eligible for a third injection,"" says Marc Peeters. ""Possibly cancer patients would benefit from a third vaccine dose,"" Sciensano researcher Mieke Goossens also said. ""Further research will reveal whether they produce a greater amount of antibodies that way."" The effect of such a third prick will be studied further in the coming months.

Netherlands Mediagenic disappearances & royal scoop: who is Peter R. de Vries, Holland's best-known crime journalist? 18 min De Vries is following the case closely: he not only attends the trials of the kidnappers and brothers-in-law Cor van Hout and Willem Holleeder, but also stays in the same hotels where the men were placed under arrest. De Vries is writing the book ""The Kidnapping of Alfred Heineken"" about the case, based on several interviews with Van Hout and Holleeder. They both want to talk to de Vries only on the condition that the interviews remain secret until after their trial. A promise de Vries keeps: the book will not be published until 1987. De Vries became close friends with Van Hout over the years, to the extent that after his death in 2003 he had an obituary placed in De Telegraaf, with the telling text ""for the most extraordinary man I have met."" In 2009, it appears that de Vries helped financially reward Van Hout for his candor in the book about Heineken's kidnapping. He lets him share in the profits. Something de Vries confirms, and by his own admission, has no regrets about. The so-called ""Putten murder case"" is a dossier into which de Vries bites like a pit bull. He devotes more than 40 broadcasts of his crime program to it. At the hands of de Vries, it will be revealed that Wilco Viets and Herman du Bois, both in jail for the rape and murder of flight attendant Christel Ambrosius, were wrongly convicted. They were released in 2002, having already served two-thirds of their 10-year sentence. They were even acquitted on appeal, which is particularly exceptional. In 2008, a new suspect is arrested. DNA testing indicates a match, sentencing the man to 18 years in prison after all. De Vries called the moment of the arrest at the police press conference ""the best day in his career as a crime reporter."" From 1995 to 2012, de Vries had his own program on Dutch commercial television, ""Peter R. de Vries, crime reporter"" . In it, both new cases and so-called cold cases - that is, old unsolved crimes - are re-examined on the basis of reconstructions. And that regularly produces results. For his program, de Vries wins an International Emmy Award, one of the most prestigious television awards. He will receive that award specifically for one of the episodes about the 2006 Natalee Holloway case, the American girl who disappeared without a trace in Aruba after meeting Dutchman Joran van der Sloot. For his program, de Vries succeeds in eliciting a crucial confession about his involvement from van der Sloot through numerous conversations with a confidant, portrayed with hidden cameras and microphones in the car. Van der Sloot admits in so many words that he dumped Holloway's corpse. The case is being reopened, and is getting a lot of media attention in the US. According to the Dutch Stichting Kijkonderzoek, this broadcast featuring the confession of Joran van der Sloot was watched by 7 million people: still a record for a non-sports program on a Dutch commercial channel. And then there is the Bruinsma case, which momentarily rocked the Dutch royal house. When Dutch Prince Friso announced his engagement to Mabel Wisse Smit in 2003, it became known that she had a past relationship with drug lord Klaas Bruinsma. Wisse Smit does not deny that she had contact with him, but rather that it was a love affair. She allegedly cut off all contact when she found out what business Bruinsma was involved in. Also, Prince Friso would have been aware of his future wife's past from the beginning of their relationship. But Peter R. de Vries is airing an interview with Charlie da Silva, a former bodyguard of Bruinsma. This sheds new light on the case, because da Silva that Wisse Smit was indeed the great love of Bruinsma. Even before the broadcast, Wisse Smit sent out a statement denying it. More details about the affair of the future Dutch princess and the drug lord will follow in a second televised episode. By the way, in the early 1990s de Vries and Bruinsma were regularly spotted together: so both men know each other as well. The case is causing a stir in the Netherlands, although Queen Beatrix continues to support her future daughter-in-law. However, no consent bill is filed for the marriage, which means so much that Prince Friso will lose his right as heir to the throne when he marries Mabel Wisse Smit in April 2004. And so it came to pass: Prince Friso prefers love to the throne.

Africa Experts Chamber committee Belgian colonial past: ""Belgium must assume its historical responsibility"" 19:18 In the special House committee looking into our colonial past, also known as the Congressional Committee, the experts presented their preliminary report. They offered tools to acknowledge and process the past, together with Congolese, Rwandans and Burundians in Belgium and at home. For some a process of years, others do not want an endless debate. There is little appetite for reparations. Committee Chairman Wouter De Vriendt of Green had to watch the session from home due to corona. ""Everything passes, except the past."" The sentence that now also adorns the wall of the renovated AfricaMuseum is by Professor Emeritus Luc Huyse, and is about the ""phantom pain"" that people of later generations still experience for injustices done to their ancestors. Jurist Martien Schotsmans of the expert committee cited the phrase to formulate her recommendations on how Belgium can compensate the victims of colonial rule and heal the wounds. That the Belgian colonial system committed serious misdeeds, experts agree. Both under the reign of King Leopold II and during the era of Belgian Congo and after the independence of Congo, Rwanda and Burundi - then Rwanda-Urundi - the colonized peoples were physically, economically and psychologically exploited, historians and other experts say. For them, it is high time Belgium took its historical responsibility for this. The expert committee gave a number of recommendations for MPs to work on now with their report. That their work of nearly 700 pages has gaps due to lack of time, they themselves admit. ""For example, the situation in Rwanda and Burundi has not been adequately explained, nor has the important role of the Catholic Church been examined,"" said historian Sara Van Beurden. The committee requests additional time to work on this. The experts' recommendations include recovery for affected populations and individuals. ""That cannot be reduced to mere financial compensation, apologies or the return of art objects,"" legal expert Martien Schotsmans said in nuance. ""It should be a comprehensive recovery program in consultation with everyone. ""The basis is that truth is recognized. This is followed by talking to the target groups, such as in hearings or through questioning, and the final goal is so-called ""outreach"": a social debate about colonialism and its consequences, such as racism. Only then will you create a support base to work on long-term recovery."" But like the experts themselves, opinions vary within the House committee. The recommendation of certain experts, for example, to allow regularization of sans-papiers from the countries concerned, or to engage in positive discrimination, was criticized. Several MPs also commented on the ""fragmented"" and ""incoherent"" nature of the report and the lack of consensus among the experts. But the financial damages advocated by art historian Anne Wetsi Mpoma are particularly controversial. Vooruit and CD&V are taking a wait-and-see approach; Vlaams Belang, N-VA and Open VLD think it's a bridge too far. Today's Belgians are not to blame. We cannot ask today's Belgians to pay for a past they did not choose to have The experts want the work of the special House committee to be an inclusive and transparent process that should ultimately build support for reconciliation. CD&V MP Els Van Hoof calls this report ""one of the cornerstones to move forward on and hear many more voices and look at other angles."" Goedele Liekens of Open VLD does not want it to become an endless process that leads to nothing.

Dutch in US over cold: stoking for a month and tape on doors 22:07 in Foreign Due to severe cold and punishing winds sweeping across the United States, tens of millions of Americans are facing weather warnings. Don't hit the road, avoid outdoor activities and protect people, pets, pipes and plants - the U.S. Weather Service refers to it as ""the four p's"": people pets pipes and plants . Many tens of millions of Americans are currently facing advisories like this as severe cold and punishing winds sweep across the United States. Warnings have been issued in more than half the country for extremely low temperatures, among other things. According to the weather service, it is not often that so many warnings are in effect at the same time. Special ""warming shelters"" have been set up in several places around the country for homeless people. More than 1.4 million Americans are without power, especially in the eastern states. Thousands of flights and dozens of train trips have also been canceled due to the winter weather, throwing millions of people's Christmas schedules into disarray. ""Christmas is canceled,"" a New York State resident tells CNN . ""All my family and friends agreed that that was safer."" We spoke to three Dutch people living in the U.S. about their experiences in the cold. They agree that the current cold is not unique, but does have one thing that makes the feeling extra intense: icy wind. Blizzard warnings are being issued in some areas of Illinois. But in Adair, the hamlet where Dutchman Barend Wurth has lived for five years, the snow is not too bad. ""It is especially very cold,"" he says of the temperature of -22 degrees, which feels like about -38. ""I live in an old farmhouse and really have to make sure all the doors are closed. Before that, I even sealed the outside doors with tape."" But the tape doesn't keep out all the cold. ""On the tape now there is a layer of ice. I have a hat on in the house and am pretty stoked. Yesterday, today and tomorrow morning, I am expected to consume a monthly amount. That's a problem for many people here, because of the high energy prices."" Wurth only taped the doors on the northwest side of his home, where the wind comes from. Because it is mostly the wind that makes it cold, he says. ""In 2019, it was also incredibly cold here, but then there was less wind. When you go outside now, the first breath just hurts. The wind makes it unbearable and dangerous."" Erna Moraine also says it: the wind makes the big difference. Dutch has experienced several (very) cold spells in the 40 years she has lived in the United States. ""And certainly winters with days like this, with lots of snow, wind and cold. But as extreme as now, with that wind chill of -38 degrees, that is life-threatening. You can't expose your bare skin to that, including your face. And I think that makes it different now."" A walk outside is not justified with the current weather conditions, Moraine said. ""So we just walked around the mall,"" she says. ""But many stores do now have notices hanging on the door that they are closed or closing early because of the weather."" Frank van den Berge, who has lived in the United States since 1988, also sees the positive aspects of winter weather. ""The snow blows across the roads here, you can hear the wind through the windows. It does give a kind of Christmas atmosphere."" The Dutch American is used to cold, though. ""It's often cold here in Wisconsin in the winter and there's often snow, actually always. If the wind had not been there, it would not have been so abnormal and obstructive."" At Van den Berge in Brookfield, it is currently about -23 degrees. ""You dress on it, with a warm coat, hat or balaclava, where only your eyes and mouth are visible."" Like Barend Wurth, Van den Berge has his doors taped shut. ""But I put that tape over the cracks every winter, against drafts. As a Dutchman, you remain frugal anyway.""

Air attack Hawija Who knew what and at what time? The question arose in the House of Representatives as to whether the granting of the Iraq mission played a role in the concealment of information. How is it that in 2015 no one - Prime Minister Mark Rutte first and foremost - was alarmed by the Dutch bombing of Iraqi Hawija, where it was clear from the outset that there would have been more damage, and ""probably"" civilian casualties? That question was asked, in many guises, on Wednesday evening by all parties as well as government parties D66 and ChristenUnie to Prime Minister Rutte (VVD) and Minister Ank Bijleveld (Defense, CDA). In the first part of the debate about the civilian casualties that occurred in Hawija and about who knew what about them and at what time, the House of Representatives focused mainly on Rutte. But the ""culture of silence"" at the Ministry of Defense was also discussed (PvdA), Prime Minister Rutte's ""selective dementia"" (Denk) and the question of whether ""this cabinet wants to know the truth"" (SP). D66 asked the minister to still investigate the exact number of civilian deaths that occurred in 2015. GroenLinks came up with new facts: because on June 19, 2015, ten days after then Defense Minister Jeanine Hennis (VVD) was briefed on the damage caused by the Dutch bombing, the then-Rutte II cabinet sent a letter to the House of Representatives, announcing the extension of the Dutch contribution to the anti-IS coalition in Iraq. ""Was extending the mission more important than sharing the truth?"" , asked Jesse Klaver. Because that knowledge, which was not mentioned in the overview Bijleveld sent to the House of Representatives earlier, shines new light on the context of the time: that extension letter shows that the Council of Ministers in June 2015 discussed with certainty the Dutch contribution in Iraq. Did the civilian deaths come up there? No, Rutte said stellar, as he began to answer the House. The prime minister denied that information was deliberately withheld from the House with the aim of extending the mission in Iraq. Even after Joël Voordewind of coalition party ChristenUnie said so. ""There is no cover-up."" Rutte went on to say, ""I can't fake memories I don't have."" Shortly thereafter, NRC went to print. The stakes were clearly higher, in this debate. The plenary chamber of the House of Representatives was fuller: there were more MPs present, more photographers, more audience. Ank Bijleveld had thought carefully: three weeks ago she was still wearing a bright blouse during the first debate on Hawija, on Wednesday night she sat in black in ""box K. The Labour Party was also criticized. Because ministers from that party (Bert Koenders, then Foreign Affairs Minister, and Lilianne Ploumen, then Minister of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation) also signed with Hennis on June 23, 2015, the letter containing incorrect information to the House. ""You have a hundred pounds of butter on your head,"" Geert Wilders (PVV) reproached the Labour Party. It was this same Wilders who did most of the opposition, for the first few hours. As the only group chairman, he interrupted the governing parties during their contribution with questions about the stability of the coalition and pointed out delicately the mutual discord between governing parties VVD, CDA, D66 and ChristenUnie. As on ChristenUnie frontman Gert-Jan Segers, who told NU.nl about Rutte forgetting information about civilian casualties, ""I do think I would have remembered."" Bijleveld, according to Wilders, would have ""with twinkling eyes"" involved Rutte in the issue. D66 MP Salima Belhaj bitched that her party was committing ""bread theft."" ""You make us redundant as an opposition."" ""This is about war,"" Belhaj responded. ""I'm trying to deal with this seriously, I want to find out what happened."" This debate will only be the beginning of that.

Terrorism funding Chairman charity foundation suspected of IS funding The World Wide Relief foundation held benefit events for victims of the Syrian civil war. In reality, according to the prosecution, they funneled the donations to IS. A major terrorism financing investigation for which the Justice Department arrested six men in November revolves around the Hilversum-based charity World Wide Relief. In addition to the foreman of that foundation, Muslim preacher Fouad el B. , it now appears that chairman Mohamed el A. has also been arrested in the case. This was confirmed by his lawyer Jan Boone. The prosecution had so far only announced that six men had been arrested in the Netherlands and Belgium, without specifying who they were or which foundation they were affiliated with. World Wide Relief held benefit events at mosques for victims of the Syrian civil war between 2013 and 2015. In reality, according to the prosecution, they funneled the donations to terror movement IS. A sum of two tons was allegedly withdrawn in cash and taken to fighters in Syria. The suspects were released after questioning by the prosecution pending the progress of the investigation. According to attorney Boone, this indicates that the case has little merit. ""If you release someone two days after his arrest, you obviously don't have a reasonable suspicion of guilt. They just can't make the case hard."" The prosecution, however, informs that the investigation is still ""ongoing"" and that a final case report is awaited. The suspects may await the course of the investigation at liberty for the time being. ""We always weigh whether it is necessary for the investigation that suspects be detained,"" a spokesman said. Longstanding question marks. Chairman Mohamed El A. denies all allegations, says attorney Boone. ""My client arranged for blankets and mattresses to head toward the border to Syria. Whether those blankets were for IS, I don't know. But even that would not be punishable. The foundation gave those blankets because they saw that people in Syria were in the terrible cold."" However, he invoked his right to remain silent in police questioning. Boone: ""Justice just has to prove otherwise. He doesn't have to declare against himself, does he?"" There had long been question marks about World Wide Relief's actions. For example, the Facebook pages of IS sympathizers called for people to donate money to the foundation. Boone says he knows nothing about that. ""If so, that does seem to me to be a reason for the government to look at what this foundation is doing. But not this way: with arrests without anything concrete in hand.""

Copyright 2020 The Associated Press. All rights reserved Protest against racism and police brutality US President Donald Trump signs executive order on police reform, will it make a difference? Tue Jun 16 20:53 The wave of protests following the death of George Floyd in the United States demanded a thorough reform of the police in the United States. President Donald Trump has now proposed new measures for the first time and signed an executive order on the matter. Thus, the controversial chokehold would no longer be allowed. But observers believe this decree will change very little in practice. Since the death of black American George Floyd on May 25 in Minneapolis, USA, protests have erupted to denounce racism and police brutality. US President Donald Trump has now signed an executive order seeking limited law enforcement reform. In this way, Trump wants to capitalize on the ongoing wave of protests. Striking: the controversial chokehold or neck clamp ( chokehold is the term Trump used) that took the life of George Floyd in Minneapolis would now only be allowed ""when an officer's life is in danger."" The US president also called on law enforcement agencies to adopt ""the strictest professional standards."" At the same time, President Trump reiterated the importance of what he calls ""law and order,"" to quickly restore order to his country. ""Americans want and demand that,"" it sounded. ""Some don't even know they want it, yet they want it. The numerous demonstrations in the United States also drew attention to underlying racism among police departments. The decree says nothing about that. Nor did the president broach the subject of racism during the ceremony. He did express his condolences to the families of victims. The president also said in his speech in the Rose Garden - that's the garden near the Oval Office in the White House in Washington that the vast majority of agents do their jobs flawlessly. ""They are in great danger of helping people they have never met,"" the president said. Trump does want reforms in police training. And there will be a registry, keeping track of the names of agents who go over the line. Yet the decree will not immediately change much in practice. The decree describes the major principles to be pursued. Many police departments in the United States are organized locally, by city and state. These follow their own rules; the presidential decree can only outline a framework. The Black Lives Matter protest movement will no doubt also not see in this decree the great leap forward that protesters have been demanding for weeks.

Flemish companies export parts for this A400M Middle East Flemish government in court for ""arms exports to Turkey"" 56 min The Flemish government says these are parts that are also used in civilian Airbus aircraft. Even according to Europe, that is not considered arms exports. A writ of summons against the Flemish government is being filed today in the court of first instance by Peace Action with the support of Amnesty International Belgium. The organizations want the Flemish government to stop exporting parts for Turkish military aircraft. Specifically, these are parts such as nuts and bolts and wing parts. Not everything supplied to a foreign military is simply labeled ""arms export."" ""Take a Flemish company that would make ballpoint pens. Suppose that were to receive an order from a foreign military, would those ballpoint pens fall under arms export? Of course not,"" said one person involved in the case. ""We do, of course, consider weapons, or parts of weapons, to be 'arms exports,'"" he said. Already since 2013, Belgian arms companies Asco Industries, Sonaca and Safran Aero Boosters have been supplying parts of the engine, wings and landing gear of the Turkish A400M military transport aircraft. That plane plays a role in supplying weapons and mercenaries for armed conflicts in Libya and Azerbaijan. Those supplies violate international arms embargoes on those countries. The question, of course, is what that has to do with Flemish exports of parts to Franco-German aircraft maker Airbus. The parts made by Flemish companies are not always specifically designed for military use. They are often part of the wings of almost all of Airbus' civilian aircraft, so we don't know if the specific nuts or bolts will end up in which aircraft. Moreover, the specific device, the A400M, is also being delivered to quite a few European countries, including Belgium itself. Our country co-developed the military transport aircraft, and therefore may also co-supply parts for the aircraft. According to Flemish and European regulations, the Flemish, Walloon and Brussels companies produce non-essential parts (of components) of the A400M. So these are parts (of parts) that can also be found in civilian aircraft in slightly modified form, including the slabs and wing parts. Shouldn't those companies know who the end customer is for their parts? "" European Directive 2009/43 explicitly prohibits restrictions on intra-European trade of non-essential components. Thus, the reporting requirement cited by Peace Action and Amnesty does not apply in this case either."" says a Flemish official close to the case. ""Flanders has actually been one of the toughest students in Europe's 'arms export class' for some time now"" says the person involved. ""Although of course that is not so difficult for us, Flanders actually has little or no real arms industry. In Wallonia, of course, with companies like FN and John Cockerill, it is different."" Jan Jambon, as authorized Prime Minister, already received a packet of questions on the matter: ""I stand by my intention to refuse, until further notice, all applications for the export of defense-related products to Turkey, as well as applications for shipments with established end-use in Turkey, obviously within the contours of the Arms Trade Decree and applicable European Regulations."" But for the parts of the A400M, he does have a different consideration: ""The parts supplied by Flemish companies are not piecework for the Turkish Air Force or any user of the A400M aircraft. It is about non-essential parts that are produced in bulk and delivered to another supplier for integration into another part; so there is also no delivery to the system integrator."" Says Jambon."" ""That is a fundamental difference from deliveries of finished systems to an operational user or of main components to a system integrator, in which we could effectively apply the restrictions you are asking for."" he said.

My future ""Adding Emotion to Tons of Moving Steel. It sounds strange, but I seek that tension. Plans, opportunities, choices, ambitions. In this series, people tell how they envision their coming years. This week: an ex-convict looking to pick up his life again. 'Technology is a dragon. It is a many-headed monster, like the Hydra of Lerna from Greek mythology. Hercules had to defeat that dragon. For every head he chopped off, two grew back. ""That's technology. Every so-called solution creates problems that were not there before. Now, on balance, what have these so-called technological innovations achieved? Convenience and comfort. Nothing more. And what has technology unleashed? A sickened atmosphere, deforestation, polluted water. ""Ten years I worked in the Internet business. I was successful, in that world. I was COO, Chief Operating Officer , boy ... It means: stress, because you promise 4.5 million euros of profit, while you risk ending the year with 3.6 million. ""Big tech is a megalomaniac industry. Mark Zuckerberg hired four thousand of the very smartest girls and boys to build his metaverse. So those overpaid talents are no longer available to solve problems that benefit the world. That sector is full of supposedly limitless but mostly useless innovations. ""Seven years ago I said to my boss: I'm quitting my job, I want to become a visual artist. I was expecting a difficult conversation. It didn't become that, quite the contrary. He asked, ""What do you need to make that switch? I was given a kind of basic income for two years. ""I was analytical and creative as a child. Choosing a course of study was difficult: saxophone at the conservatory, or to TU in Delft? I come from a close-knit Brabant field hockey family of entrepreneurs and general practitioners. Then you learn that you have to work for your money; art is fun in your spare time. So I became an engineer. ""As an artist, I remain fully engaged with technology. Tech is my language. Miracles I want to make with it. I develop robots, with which I want to make beauty visible and tangible. In about three years from now, I will have a play on stage that is played entirely by robots. That's my dream right now. ""Adding emotion to tons of moving steel. It sounds strange, but I seek that tension. I want to let opposites live on so that something new, something beautiful is created. ""With my work, I want to say, 'We have a choice! We don't have to have our groceries delivered to our homes within minutes. Stop doing that! We can go to Mars, but why would we want to? We don't always need to know everything about everyone immediately, that phone can just be turned off! ""I admit it: I am not free of tech addiction myself. The other day I went for a walk from Amsterdam East to West. I had forgotten my phone. I got lost. Then I thought: the sun is now in the southwest, so I have to go that way. It felt like a victory when I got out where I wanted to be. Super-childish, actually. ""At our house, there is a bin by the front door. For the smartphones, as we come in. Our children are now eight and ten. I don't know how long we can keep these things out of our family life. ""I am not a drammer. I do have a picture of how I want to live and coexist. At home, we strive to form a family that is able to enjoy, without avoiding problems. Just, sitting together, talking to each other, peeling an apple. ""Whether I'm happy now, I'm not sure. This is because I am unbridledly curious. There are still so many plans in my head that need to get out. I do know that I am now free to make my own choices. That alone feels SO much better than making shareholders rich.""

Pee Pass: 'A student with a full bladder can't concentrate anyway' A survey of some directors reveals that medically motivated toilet licenses are rather rare. 'The few students who have a medical certificate don't run with it,' says director An Reyskens of Don Bosco Genk. Although many schools do have a regulatory framework for plasma moments. So too at the GO! Technical Atheneum in Halle, where Maggy Van Keerbergen heads. 'Our students must have a pass if they want to go to the restroom during class. Each teacher has such a card with which he or she gives formal permission to students. That way we also know immediately why a student wanders through the hallways during classes. At Sint-Jozef College in Aarschot, principal Mattias Paglialunga tries to concentrate sanitary traffic as much as possible during the break. 'We don't have pee passes, but during classes almost all the restroom doors close.' Almost everywhere, the same reasoning rings true. Structured potty breaks help maintain order in school. 'You know how that goes,' says Reyskens. 'As soon as someone wants to go to the bathroom, suddenly the whole class has to.' According to Van Keerbergen, it is mainly a matter of keeping an overview. 'Because the teacher's name is on our passes, we know right away who the frequent urinators are and if there is a lesson pattern in toilet visits. Besides, you just don't have control anymore when students can walk in and out freely. Over the past two years, Verhenne has watched the lack of control turn into increasing vandalism. 'It used to be less pronounced, but these days the boys' toilets in particular look rather unbecoming.' The relatively limited damage also creates logistical problems, Verhenne said. 'Fortunately, it sticks to mischief like chocolate on the toilet doors, or scattering unwound rolls of toilet paper around. We have no manpower to guard the toilets, so to prevent it from escalating we lock doors during classes. Confidence. What if the need is really high? All of our respondents indicated that there is never an absolute ban. ""Nor is that desirable,"" believes Dimitri Meurrens of the Institute Maris Stella - Sint Agnes in Borgerhout. 'You can't stop that anyway. Yes, it's annoying when a teacher has to interrupt his lesson repeatedly, but a student with a full bladder can't concentrate anyway. How do you distinguish the balorigen from the needy? Verhenne: I assume my teachers know their students. So what if they make an error in judgment? Missing is human. Paglialunga advocates dialogue. 'We prefer a conversation when things do go wrong. You want to understand why a student is trying to escape classes. Meurrens is of the same opinion. 'It comes down to asking questions. Does a student feel bad? Does he not like going to school? Is there something else going on? At the end of the day, it's a matter of trust.
